conflicts.issue: Wiley and Elizabeth Forbes House Local Historic Landmark Designation (LD150002)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 on designating the Wiley and Elizabeth Forbes House at 3307 Devon Road as a local historic landmark, an item for which the City Manager had added a fiscal impact analysis prior to the vote. Mayor Bill Bell, Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden, Steve Schewel, Eddie Davis, and Don Moffitt voted in favor, while Eugene Brown and Diane Catotti voted against.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve local historic landmark designation for 3307 Devon Road
side_a_arguments: Preserves the architectural integrity of one of the first 20 structures built in Hope Valley.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose local historic landmark designation for 3307 Devon Road
side_b_arguments: Voted no following addition of the fiscal impact analysis (specific floor remarks omitted in transcript digest gap).
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-2

conflicts.issue: US 70 Self Storage Center Rezoning (Z1400020)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-2 to approve rezoning 7.55 acres on US 70 Highway to IL(D) for a self-storage facility despite a 1-10 Planning Commission denial recommendation. Mayor Bill Bell, Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden, Eugene Brown, Steve Schewel, and Don Moffitt voted in favor after the applicant proffered a permanent access easement covenant, while Diane Catotti and Eddie Davis voted no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the US 70 Self Storage Center rezoning with the revised access easement commitment
side_a_arguments: Staff determined the proposal complied with UDO and policy provisions, including US 70 right-of-way dedication and Page Road reservation.
The applicant's newly proffered covenant requiring a recorded permanent access easement prior to building permit or certificate of occupancy addressed key access concerns (cited by Don Moffitt).
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose rezoning 7.55 acres to IL(D) for a self-storage facility
side_b_arguments: Voted no on the rezoning following a 1-10 Planning Commission denial recommendation (Don Moffitt also noted discomfort with severing half of an existing site development plan before ultimately voting yes).
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-2

conflicts.issue: Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard Lane Reconfiguration (3-Lane Road Diet vs. 5-Lane Status Quo / Delay)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 over whether to adopt staff's proposed three-lane bike/parking reconfiguration immediately or accept NCDOT resurfacing while deferring the striping decision due to business-owner opposition.
conflicts.side_a_position: Proceed with NCDOT-funded resurfacing immediately and defer the striping decision until late June to allow further discussion with affected businesses.
side_a_arguments: Durham should not turn down state NCDOT resurfacing funding for a deteriorated corridor.
A large share of local business owners along the short corridor opposed the lane reduction and felt insufficiently consulted, signaling a communication breakdown.
The proposed plan adds only 21 parking spaces, and council still has until the end of June to finalize striping.
conflicts.side_b_position: Decide the striping configuration directly rather than adopting a convoluted deferral, with supporters of the 3-lane plan arguing delay jeopardizes safety and parking improvements.
side_b_arguments: Slowing traffic and adding bike lanes and parking makes pulling out of corridor restaurants and shops safer and will attract more customers.
Deferring to an unspecified later vote is procedurally convoluted and risks missing NCDOT's summer contract deadline or overloading the next 63-item agenda.
Council should vote directly up-or-down on the three-lane vs. five-lane striping rather than deferring.
conflicts.resolution: Eugene Brown's substitute-to-the-substitute motion to proceed with NCDOT resurfacing and revisit striping later passed 4-3 (Ayes: Bell, Cole-McFadden, Brown, Davis; Nays: Catotti, Moffitt, Schewel).

conflicts.issue: Inclusion of Sheriff's Stolen Firearms Felony Elevation and 72-Month Mandatory Minimum in 2015 Legislative Agenda
conflicts.summary: Council divided 3-4 over whether to endorse the Durham County Sheriff's proposal asking the General Assembly to elevate stolen firearm offenses from Class H to Class E felony and impose a mandatory 72-month minimum prison term when a stolen firearm is used in another felony.
conflicts.side_a_position: Endorse the Sheriff's stolen firearm penalty enhancement in the city's 2015 legislative package to deter gun thefts and violence.
side_a_arguments: Stolen firearms and residential burglaries (up 30-40%, including stolen gun safes) feed street-level gun violence, aggravated assaults, and homicides in Durham.
Stealing a firearm is an intentional act whose purpose is typically resale or criminal use, warranting tougher Class E felony status and incapacitation.
Supporting the Sheriff sends a clear community message that gun violence is intolerable.
conflicts.side_b_position: Decline to add the Sheriff's sentencing enhancement to the city's legislative agenda.
side_b_arguments: Elevating property theft of a firearm to Class E disrupts North Carolina's structured sentencing grid by equating theft with violent crimes against persons.
A mandatory 72-month minimum eliminates judicial discretion contrary to national sentencing reform trends and carries high incarceration costs without evidence of deterrence.
The Sheriff had not consulted the NC Sentencing Commission, lacked crime-reduction projections, and existing 2013 firearm sentencing enhancements have not yet been evaluated.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to add the Sheriff's proposal to the legislative agenda failed 3-4; the remaining 2015 legislative agenda was then approved 6-0.

conflicts.issue: Administrative Approval of Unipole Wireless Towers Ahead of Comprehensive WCF Revisions (TC1400004)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 1-6 to reject a private text amendment allowing unipole ('slick stick') cell towers via administrative approval in non-residential districts, choosing instead to wait for the broader wireless communication facility ordinance overhaul (TC120013).
conflicts.side_a_position: Wait for comprehensive wireless ordinance revisions (TC120013) and retain Special Use Permit public hearings.
side_a_arguments: Approving a single-company text amendment would short-circuit months of stakeholder engagement by JCCPC, staff, and neighborhood groups on TC120013.
The comprehensive overhaul is expected to require larger lots and greater setbacks than the existing UDO.
The applicant already had the option to seek a Special Use Permit before the Board of Adjustment for the specific Durham Tech site.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve administrative approval for unipoles in non-residential zones immediately.
side_b_arguments: Waiting six months for TC120013 delays improved cellular coverage and 911 access near Durham Tech.
Unipoles conceal antennas internally and are far less visually obtrusive than monopines, which are already administratively permitted.
conflicts.resolution: Failed 1-6; Council adopted the denial consistency statement 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Erwin Terrace at LaSalle Street Compact Neighborhood Tier Expansion and Transit-Area Affordable Housing (A130010)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 in approving a Comprehensive Plan amendment expanding the Compact Neighborhood Tier at Erwin Road and LaSalle Street without a binding 15% affordable housing commitment in new construction.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Compact Neighborhood Tier expansion now without delaying for the city's affordable housing toolbox.
side_a_arguments: Approximately 2,030 units (79.5%) within a half-mile of the proposed LaSalle Street station are already affordable at 60% AMI, well above Council's 15% aggregate goal.
Lenders would not finance a complex wrapped parking deck mixed-use development with mandatory 15% below-market units, and North Carolina law prohibits mandatory inclusionary zoning.

Delaying an established local developer who applied before the May 2014 resolution—and proffered $25,000 for the housing toolbox plus a Poplar Manor redevelopment pause—would jeopardize jobs, tax base, and light rail density.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer or reject piecemeal tier expansion until holistic station-area planning and stronger long-term affordable housing commitments are in place.
side_b_arguments: Current market-rate affordability around Duke Manor and Poplar Manor is not permanently protected and rents are already rising ahead of light rail.
Expanding the Compact Neighborhood Tier parcel-by-parcel undermines the comprehensive SASI station-area planning and affordable housing toolkit process underway for January 2015.
Keeping the hearing open could allow the developer to craft a longer-term preservation commitment for Poplar Manor once the city's incentive toolbox is ready.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-2; Council later voted 7-0 for the companion rezoning (Z130031) after the developer extended the Poplar Manor hold to 18 months and added a $23,000 DPS contribution.

conflicts.issue: Decommitting Trail Connections in Harmony Road II / Chamberlain Subdivision (Z1400008)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 over whether to release Standard Pacific from a 2006 committed element to build an asphalt trail connecting Chamberlain to Woodcroft's trail system and a southern mulch trail.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve removing the trail commitments because Woodcroft refused an off-site easement and Chamberlain residents negotiated a $75,000 recreation fund compromise.
side_a_arguments: Woodcroft Community Association formally rejected four to six proposed alignments across its private property.
Chamberlain residents agreed to redirect the $75,000 trail budget (net of legal/consulting costs) toward neighborhood recreation amenities.
Existing zoning lacked a timing trigger, and off-site easements beyond a developer's property boundary should not be enforced.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose decommitting the trails in order to preserve critical off-road pedestrian/bicycle connectivity to Southwest Elementary School and the Third Fork Creek Trail.
side_b_arguments: BPAC and residents rely on off-road trail links rather than forcing children onto city streets.
Removing the developer's commitment pushes the eventual cost of completing the Third Fork Creek tributary trail onto city taxpayers.
Woodcroft itself benefited from visionary trails, and the developer should pursue another alignment (such as toward Brindhurst/Tall Oaks) or mediation.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 5-2 (Catotti and Schewel voting no), removing the trail commitments.

conflicts.issue: Repeal of the $1.80/Month Solid Waste Collection Fee vs. Property Tax Replacement (Item 10D & Final Budget)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 on repealing the $1.80/month solid waste collection fee and replacing its $1.4 million revenue with property taxes, leading Eugene Brown to vote no (6-1) on the final overall budget.
conflicts.side_a_position: Repeal the flat $1.80/month ($21.60/year) solid waste fee and fund the $1.4 million through the property tax rate.
side_a_arguments: A flat per-household fee is regressive, charging a $75,000 homeowner or low-income renter the same $21.60/year as a $500,000 homeowner.
Any homeowner below ~$370,000 in assessed value—and single-family/duplex renters who pay $0 directly under property tax—pays less under Option 1.
Keeping the fee would require a 56% fee hike next year to cover a projected $800,000 solid waste shortfall.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain the $1.80/month solid waste user fee to stabilize the solid waste enterprise fund and avoid raising property taxes.
side_b_arguments: The $20 million solid waste fund already receives $9.6 million in general-fund property tax subsidies from all property owners, including businesses and multi-family residents without city pickup.
Like DATA bus fares, a modest $1.80/month user fee for households receiving collection service is not regressive, and DSS assistance covers hardship cases.
Replacing the fee plus county/other increases risks giving Durham the highest municipal property tax rate among North Carolina's largest cities, hurting competitiveness.
conflicts.resolution: Option 1 repeal passed 4-3; the remaining FY 2014-15 budget ordinances then passed 6-1 with Eugene Brown dissenting because the final budget incorporated the fee repeal.

conflicts.issue: Phillips Research Park Apartments Impact Fee Appeal – Strict Code Enforcement vs. Equitable Tolling for Neighbor Litigation Delays
conflicts.summary: Council split 6-1 in upholding staff's denial of Phillips Research Park Apartments' appeal of a $108,000 impact fee increase incurred after a competitor's zoning appeals froze the project from 2008 until building permits were filed under the higher 2009 fee schedule, with Eugene Brown dissenting and Eddie Davis exploring a compromise split.
conflicts.side_a_position: Uphold the Impact Fee Appeal Committee and staff determination applying the July 1, 2009 impact fee schedule in effect when the building permit application was submitted.
side_a_arguments: City Code strictly mandates that impact fees be calculated at the time a completed building permit application is submitted (here 2010-2011), leaving Council and the Impact Fee Appeal Committee no legal authority to retroactively apply expired 2008 rates.
While the neighboring competitor's appeals caused hardship, Planning staff followed mandatory UDO stay provisions and the application also sat with the developer for extended periods.
Granting retroactive fee relief to one developer could expose the city to legal challenges and refund demands from other developers affected by fee or regulatory changes.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer the appeal back to the City Manager rather than upholding the higher 2009 fee assessment, citing inadequate Planning Department communication and notification to the developer.
side_b_arguments: Planning staff failed to communicate effectively with the developer regarding the impact fee change and could have communicated more forcefully regarding the neighboring owner's interconnection obligations.

Because the developer relied on 2007 staff reliance letters, closed a $23 million loan in 2008, and was stalled by third-party litigation outside its control, Council should send the matter back to the Manager for further review rather than deny relief.
conflicts.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel's motion to uphold the staff and Impact Fee Appeal Committee determination passed 6-1, with Councilmember Eugene Brown voting No (while Councilmember Eddie Davis noted he would have favored splitting the increase in half if legally permissible but did not offer a substitute motion after Schewel's motion carried).

conflicts.issue: Hope Valley Farms Pod BB Rezoning for Murphy USA Fuel Station & Convenience Store (Z13-0012)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 on removing a 2009 prohibition on fuel sales and convenience stores at 1051 Martin Luther King Jr. Parkway after neighboring Elm Grove Townhouse residents requested a continuance and council members scrutinized building aesthetics.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning (with an added four-sided brick exterior commitment) without further delay.
side_a_arguments: City and applicant met all statutory notification rules, including first-class letters to 45 property owners and the Elm Grove Townhouse Association.
The site has been zoned Commercial General since 2009, lies 500 feet from the nearest townhomes behind a 0.8 opacity vegetative buffer, and adds $2 million in tax base.
Applicant amended design commitments on reconsideration to mandate a brick exterior on all four walls.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose approval or delay action in light of Elm Grove neighborhood concerns.
side_b_arguments: Questioned whether affected Elm Grove townhome residents had adequate opportunity to review the proposal given their HOA board transition.
Raised compatibility and neighborhood impact concerns for the convenience store and fuel station.
conflicts.resolution: Initially passed 5-2, reconsidered 7-0 to secure a four-sided brick exterior commitment, and re-approved 5-2.

conflicts.issue: Willow Street Closing and Cul-de-Sac Street Connectivity (SC14-00018)
conflicts.summary: Council Member Don Moffitt questioned closing an unimproved segment of Willow Street to create a cul-de-sac rather than preserving a street connection to Huron Street, before joining a unanimous vote after staff and the applicant cited stream-crossing barriers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Close the 7,251-square-foot right-of-way to enable access to seven interior residential lots via a cul-de-sac.
side_a_arguments: The right-of-way has remained platted and unimproved for decades while surrounding Tuscaloosa-Lakewood streets already provide strong grid connectivity.
Extending Willow Street south or connecting out to Huron Street would require crossing a protected buffered stream.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid creating dead-end cul-de-sacs when Comprehensive Plan and UDO policies favor street connectivity.
side_b_arguments: Approving a single cul-de-sac because surrounding streets are connected undermines connectivity principles for emergency services and traffic circulation.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 7-0 after Planning staff and Jared Edens clarified both potential through-connections would require stream crossings.

conflicts.issue: UDO Text Amendment: Unipole Freestanding Wireless Communications Facilities (TC1400004)
conflicts.summary: Michael Stock of the Planning Department presented TC1400004, a privately initiated text amendment by Morningstar Law Group for Durham Tower LLC to allow unipoles ('slick sticks') administratively in non-residential districts, noting that staff preferred folding the change into the comprehensive wireless facility overhaul (TC120013) due in late winter or early spring. Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and partner Matthew Danielson argued the amendment was urgently needed to place a visually unobtrusive tower near Durham Tech without resorting to a monopine, while Dolly and Mel Fahrenbacher and Victoria Peterson opposed piecemeal changes and urged preserving Special Use Permit public hearings. Council Members Diane Catotti, Eddie Davis, and Steve Schewel opposed short-circuiting the comprehensive JCCPC and neighborhood stakeholder process, noting the applicant could seek a Special Use Permit instead. Catotti moved the item with the stated intention of voting no, seconded by Schewel, and the amendment failed 1-6 with only Don Moffitt voting in favor.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 1-6)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (1-6)

conflicts.issue: Size of Economic Development Incentive for Morris Street Phase 1 Development (C1, C2, P1)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over an economic development incentive agreement for Phase 1 of the Morris Street office, laboratory, and structured parking project near the Carmichael Building. While six members voted yes to deliver needed Class A downtown office space and structured parking, Council Member Diane Catotti voted no over the high incentive percentage.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Phase 1 Morris Street economic development incentive agreement
side_a_arguments: Downtown Class A office vacancy is only 6%, causing Durham to lose prospective employers without new office and lab space.
Structured parking is required to capitalize the multi-phase development and achieve a competitive market return.
While acknowledging the incentive percentage is high, supporters opted to approve this deal while pushing to lower future incentive percentages toward a 50-50 split as downtown strengthens.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the incentive agreement due to excessive city incentive percentage
side_b_arguments: Objected to the large city incentive percentage relative to the project and growing strength of the downtown market (referenced by supporting colleague at 01:25:45).
conflicts.resolution: Passed 6-1

conflicts.issue: Longfellow Real Estate Partners (Durham Innovation District) $5.25M Preliminary Incentive Terms
conflicts.summary: Council debated the subsidy level, year-three occupancy threshold, public park language, public parking availability, and future-phase subsidy expectations for the Durham Innovation District incentive.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the preliminary incentive agreement to catalyze Class A lab and office development on underutilized downtown parcels.
side_a_arguments: The project creates needed Class A office and high-tech lab space, attracts high-wage jobs, and increases long-term property tax revenue.
Deferring the 70% occupancy threshold until the third payment year reflects the leasing timeline for speculative lab buildings.
Staff addressed closed-session concerns regarding the proposed public park and future-phase expectations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the incentive terms as overly generous to the developer with insufficient public return and county participation.
side_b_arguments: Rebating 70% of future tax revenues over 15 years is too high.
Deferring the 70% occupancy requirement until year three is overly generous given claimed market demand.
A higher percentage of parking should be open to the public and Durham County should contribute more.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 6-1 (Diane Catotti voting No; Don Moffitt and Steve Schewel voted Aye while flagging park-access and future-phase incentive concerns).

conflicts.issue: Guglhupf Bakery Commercial Parking Expansion into Francis Street Residential Block (A14-00007 / Z14-00007)
conflicts.summary: While the Tuscaloosa-Lakewood Neighborhood Association board and Guglhupf reached a negotiated compromise allowing commercial parking across Francis Street with covenants and buffers, a nearby resident opposed breaching the residential boundary and Council Member Steve Schewel questioned the lack of binding bike-rack text commitments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the FLUM amendment and CG(D) rezoning based on negotiated buffers, building prohibition, tree preservation, and private side agreements.
side_a_arguments: Alleviates heavy overflow staff and customer parking and pedestrian safety hazards on neighborhood streets and Durham-Chapel Hill Blvd.
Includes a binding 22.5-foot vegetated buffer, decorative fencing, no-building commitment, private restrictive covenant, and TLNA board endorsement.
conflicts.side_b_position: Preserve strict backyard-to-backyard residential boundaries and require BPAC-recommended bicycle parking commitments on the parent site.
side_b_arguments: Opposing resident Susan Sewell argued commercial uses should not leap across Francis Street into residential blocks and neighborhoods should not have to negotiate piece-by-piece for buffer protections.
Council Member Steve Schewel noted the applicant declined to proffer BPAC's requested bike racks on the existing restaurant parcel in the binding development plan.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 7-0 after applicant noted UDO site plan review will require bike racks on the new parking lot and Council Member Catotti cited stringent negotiated protections.

conflicts.issue: Wireless Communications Facilities Text Amendment Scope and Suburban Height Cap (TC12-00013)
conflicts.summary: Council unanimously adopted the 2012-2015 cell tower ordinance overhaul as drafted by staff, declining to delay passage to incorporate an 85-foot height cap in suburban Rural Residential areas (recommended 8-4 by the Planning Commission) or additional resident-proposed safety and FCC upsizing safeguards.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the drafted WCF text amendment immediately and refer remaining safety and technical questions for future annual technical review.
side_a_arguments: After more than two years of work by staff, JCCPC, and citizen groups, the ordinance delivers major gains including 600-foot notice, balloon tests, gas-line setbacks, and Board of Adjustment hearings.

Five-acre minimum lot sizes and quasi-judicial BOA hearings already protect suburban RR neighborhoods, whereas an 85-foot cap could risk federal Telecommunications Act litigation or poor rural coverage.
Holding the ordinance for new drafting would cause multi-cycle delays and require re-coordination with the Board of County Commissioners.
conflicts.side_b_position: Cap tower height at 85 feet in suburban RR zones, require public hearings for all concealed towers under 60 feet, and write explicit storm-safety standards into the ordinance before adoption.
side_b_arguments: Neighborhood speakers (Fred Bauer, Al Fahrenbacher, Ms. Rudolph) warned FCC rules allow <60-foot concealed towers approved administratively to later expand significantly without neighborhood input.
Speakers cited Hurricane Sandy antenna failures and generator fuel hazards as requiring explicit structural and safety language rather than reliance on implied building codes.
Four Planning Commissioners and the InterNeighborhood Council backed an 85-foot height limit in suburban RR areas.
conflicts.resolution: Adopted 7-0 as drafted, with Council Members Schewel and Bell requesting staff follow up on remaining safety issues through JCCPC and future technical amendments.

conflicts.issue: Auto Park Center / Sheetz Commercial General Rezoning Adjacent to Lower New Hope Creek Floodplain (Z14-00011)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to rezone 6.23 acres at NC 751 and Interstate 40 from Commercial Neighborhood to Commercial General for a Sheetz convenience store and gas station, over Council Member Diane Catotti's dissent citing DOST environmental concerns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve CG(D) rezoning to allow Sheetz convenience retail, restaurant, and fuel sales near I-40.
side_a_arguments: The site sits directly across from an auto mall next to I-40 and brings jobs and private investment to Durham.
The development plan prohibits residential and electronic gaming uses, meets state natural heritage floodplain buffer guidelines, and received 12-0 Planning Commission support.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain Commercial Neighborhood zoning and oppose gasoline sales adjacent to the Lower New Hope Creek natural heritage corridor.
side_b_arguments: Echoed Durham Open Space and Trails Commission concerns about placing fuel sales directly adjacent to the exceptional-quality Lower New Hope Creek floodplain forest and steep slopes.
Neighborhood Commercial zoning remains more appropriate for the corridor than General Commercial.
conflicts.resolution: Rezoning passed 6-1 with Diane Catotti voting Nay; the statutory consistency statement subsequently passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Grandin Trace Rezoning Traffic Access on Grandale Drive (Z130035)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to approve the 54-unit Grandin Trace single-family rezoning, with Council Member Don Moffitt dissenting over all development traffic exiting onto Grandale Drive.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with required Grandale Drive right-turn lane and double-frontage landscaping.
side_a_arguments: The proposal is consistent with the Low-Density Residential future land use map and received a 10-0 Planning Commission recommendation.
The project does not reach the trip threshold for a TIA to require an off-site left-turn lane at Grandale and Barbee Road, which is already committed by 751 South.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose approval due to lack of Herndon Road access.
side_b_arguments: Routing all new subdivision traffic onto Grandale Drive without a connection to Herndon Road places the traffic burden solely on Grandale Drive.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Waffle House NC 55 Rezoning and Downstream Flooding Risks (Z140019)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to rezone 1.5 acres on NC 55 Highway for a Waffle House, with Mayor Bill Bell dissenting over downstream flooding concerns raised by a nearby homeowner.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Commercial Neighborhood rezoning subject to modern stormwater rules.
side_a_arguments: The site is designated Commercial on the Future Land Use Map and is outside the mapped floodplain.
Current Durham stormwater and Jordan/Falls Lake rules require engineered underground retention and filtration so post-development runoff does not exceed pre-development levels.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose rezoning due to flooding risks in the adjacent corridor.
side_b_arguments: Disturbing and paving land near Meridian Parkway and Henry Place risks worsening chronic flooding experienced by nearby residents.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Acquisition of East Main Street / Carpenter Motor Company Site for New Police Headquarters
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over acquiring 4.523 acres along East Main Street for ~$5.69 million (plus demolition) for a new police headquarters and 911 complex, with Eugene Brown dissenting on cost and appraisal grounds while other members supported the site while pressing for urban design, retail activation, and historic/transit trade-offs.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the GWC Properties and W.T. Wilkerson land acquisition options to secure a consolidated central East Main Street site for police and 911 operations.
side_a_arguments: Extensive site search ruled out Fayetteville Street (planned for DHA redevelopment) and showed rebuilding on the existing site was cost-prohibitive.
Police and 911 departments wholeheartedly endorse the site, and GWC tenant rents during 2015 help offset the purchase premium over appraisal.
Staff committed to public design forums to improve Main Street walkability, streetscape, and potential public-private retail partnerships.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the acquisition due to excessive cost (~$1.33M/acre plus demolition), reliance on a single appraisal, and paying 2.5x appraised value for the Hood Street parcel.
side_b_arguments: The city normally obtains two appraisals for major real estate acquisitions, whereas only one appraisal was done per property here.
Combined acquisition and $300,000-$400,000 demolition costs total roughly $6 million, representing an exceedingly high price per acre.
Public speakers also objected to demolishing the historic 1928 and 1948 Carpenter Motor Company buildings and questioned spending $6 million on a large headquarters.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-1; General Services proceeded with geotechnical/environmental due diligence and committed to public design forums and periodic Council updates.

conflicts.issue: Austin Lawrence Partners (City Center / Jack Tar) Incentive Agreement – Minimum Guaranteed Property Tax Yield vs. Capital Investment Metric
conflicts.summary: Mayor Bill Bell dissented in a 6-1 vote on the $3.97 million, 15-year incentive agreement for the City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment, insisting the contract include an absolute minimum annual property tax yield ($327,400) rather than relying solely on capital investment thresholds, while the six council members and city finance/legal staff supported approving the agreement as drafted under existing policy.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $3.97M incentive agreement immediately as drafted under existing economic development policy, relying on conservative tax assessor estimates ($60.9M assessed value) and avoiding constitutional tax-rebate risks.
side_a_arguments: Existing city policy bases incentives on qualified capital investment ($65M minimum) rather than actual tax revenue yields because directly linking incentives to tax revenues or requiring make-up payments risks violating the North Carolina Constitution's prohibition on tax rebates.

Finance staff already applied conservative buffers by basing projections on the tax assessor's $60.9M valuation (about 10% below the $65M minimum investment), capping the incentive at ~80.9% of projected property tax, and excluding ~$3.4M in projected hotel occupancy and sales taxes.
Delaying approval past April would disrupt the developer's imminent REIT financing term sheet and push back demolition and construction timelines.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hold the agreement until Thursday and amend Section 2.1 (or attach Exhibit D) to guarantee that the project generates at least $327,400 annually in general fund property tax revenue regardless of future property revaluations.
side_b_arguments: While the city's 15-year payout (~$265K/year) is fixed in dollars, future countywide property revaluations typically lower tax rates and could erode actual property tax inflows below the $327,400 projection.

Future councils paying out general fund dollars over 15 years should have contractual certainty of the minimum property tax revenue returning to the general fund rather than relying on non-binding memos or uncertain sales/hotel taxes.
conflicts.resolution: Council rejected Mayor Bell's request to hold the item until Thursday and approved the incentive agreement 6-1, with Bell voting No; City Attorney Fred Lamar agreed to examine revenue-guarantee mechanisms during the upcoming comprehensive Economic Development Policy overhaul.

conflicts.issue: Article 6 UDO Density Revisions and Impact on Transit-Oriented Growth & Affordable Housing (TC1200012)
conflicts.summary: During the public hearing on Item 15, the Inter-Neighborhood Council opposed residential density increases unrelated to transit access, and Council Members Don Moffitt and Eddie Davis scrutinized whether raising baseline densities undermined affordable housing bonuses or warranted delaying residential provisions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the revised Article 6 density adjustments and corridor bonuses as proposed by Horvath Associates and Planning staff.
side_a_arguments: Rounding fractional densities (at most 0.5 units/acre) and extending roadway bonuses to service roads and commercial/office districts encourages mixed-use redevelopment along major corridors.
Any higher density in RSM/RUM districts still requires a development plan approved by City Council, and service-road bonuses require direct access.
Density bonuses in the UDO can stack cumulatively, and affordable housing requires broader tools beyond density alone (Steve Medlin).
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay or reject the residential density provisions until density is directed toward walkable, transit-served areas and affordable housing bonuses are protected.
side_b_arguments: Allowing extra residential density outside transit corridors risks car-dependent sprawl (Pat Carstensen / Inter-Neighborhood Council).
Increasing by-right or baseline unit counts could reduce developers' incentive to use the affordable housing density bonus (questioned by Don Moffitt).
conflicts.resolution: Following staff clarifications that development plans still come before Council and that Planning will pursue non-density affordable housing incentives, Council unanimously approved TC1200012 by a 7-0 vote.

conflicts.issue: Awarding WIA Youth Contract to Out-of-County Provider Over Durham Applicant (Item 4)
conflicts.summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden dissented against awarding a Workforce Investment Act youth contract to Raleigh-based Community Partnerships, Inc. over Durham-based Operation Breakthrough.
conflicts.side_a_position: Follow the Workforce Development Board's recommendation to award the contract to Community Partnerships, Inc.
side_a_arguments: CPI scored higher overall (89 vs. 88.5) and consistently met federal and state WIA performance goals.
Workforce board members cited a recent audit of Operation Breakthrough and concerns about continuity under Operation Breakthrough's six-month intern staffing model.
conflicts.side_b_position: Prioritize Durham-based contractors and invest in mentoring local organizations rather than awarding contracts outside the city.
side_b_arguments: A half-point scoring margin (89 vs. 88.5) should not outweigh keeping public workforce dollars with a local Durham provider.
City staff should proactively mentor local firms like Operation Breakthrough so they can compete effectively for city contracts.
conflicts.resolution: Contract awarded to Community Partnerships, Inc. by a 6-1 vote.

conflicts.issue: Rescission of 11 Previously Ordered $5/Foot Petition Sidewalk Projects
conflicts.summary: Following resident testimony over pedestrian safety and consultant scoring fairness, council split 5-1 on rescinding 11 older petition sidewalk orders to transition toward the Durham Walks prioritization framework and higher $35/foot petitioner assessments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Rescind the 11 older petition orders now and revisit sidewalk funding and prioritization alternatives during the upcoming budget process.
side_a_arguments: Leaving petitions approved 7-8 years ago on the active list when they lack funding is misleading to residents.
Very limited sidewalk funds should be directed through the Durham Walks priority plan to maximize safety, school proximity, and overall connectivity.
Five of the 11 corridors remain in the Durham Walks plan and can be re-petitioned at $35/foot alongside future budget discussions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose rescinding the previously ordered neighborhood petition sidewalks.
side_b_arguments: Consultant scoring criteria unfairly penalized neighborhood projects such as Sedgwick Road in Parkwood because the adjacent park is HOA-owned rather than city-owned and the route connects to an existing school sidewalk rather than fronting the school directly.
Durham is already 'sidewalk poor' and should prioritize intra-neighborhood connectivity and citizen volunteer efforts rather than canceling approved projects.
conflicts.resolution: Resolution rescinding the 11 petition sidewalk projects passed 5-1 (Cole-McFadden excused absent), with staff directed to bring sidewalk funding and Durham Walks options back during the FY2015-16 budget process.

conflicts.issue: Hanover Point UDO Road Connection to McLamb Drive (Z1400004)
conflicts.summary: Residents along McLamb Drive, Bristolwood Drive, and Danbury Road opposed connecting Hanover Point (Willow Crest Road) to McLamb Drive due to narrow, deteriorating state-maintained roads, while Council approved the rezoning 6-0 because the connection was required by UDO connectivity rules and already dedicated in 2006.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Z1400004 rezoning to reduce density from 68 to 41 single-family homes while maintaining the previously dedicated UDO street connection.
side_a_arguments: Denying the rezoning leaves the 2006 approval intact, allowing 68 higher-density homes while still requiring the exact same McLamb Drive connection.
UDO connectivity standards mandate tying into dedicated stub roads for emergency access and interconnected neighborhoods.
Most Hanover Point traffic will travel south through modern city-standard Ashton Hall streets rather than north onto deteriorating state roads.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose connecting Willow Crest Road to McLamb Drive and direct new development traffic elsewhere until roads are upgraded.
side_b_arguments: McLamb and Bristolwood are 18-foot-wide, uncurbed 1984 tar-and-gravel state roads already disintegrating into dirt.
Cut-through commuters heading north toward Highway 98 and Wake Forest will accelerate road deterioration without developer or NCDOT repair funding.
32 neighbors signed a petition favoring use of an alternate future connector stub further from existing homes.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-0; Council advised residents to petition NCDOT (including former Durham Mayor Nick Tennyson) or consider voluntary city annexation for street maintenance.

conflicts.issue: Replacing the Solid Waste Fee with a Property Tax Increase in FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 over Don Moffitt's motion to include in the FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines a proposal to eliminate the solid waste fee (~$1.4 million) and replace it with up to 0.6 cents on the property tax rate.
conflicts.side_a_position: Include replacing the solid waste fee with up to 0.6 cents property tax in the budget guidelines for evaluation
side_a_arguments: Eliminating the flat solid waste fee in favor of property tax revenue replaces a regressive fee with a less regressive tax.
Adding the option to the budget development guidelines does not finalize the budget until June and provides staff direction to present detailed numbers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose putting replacement of the solid waste/garbage fee with a property tax into the budget guidelines
side_b_arguments: Opposed eliminating the garbage fee and shifting its cost onto property taxes.
Expressed concern that adding the provision to the guidelines signaled support for the policy change.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 4-3 (Don Moffitt grounded in favor; Bill Bell grounded among the Nays; remaining three Ayes and two Nays not individually named in transcript); subsequently incorporated into the unanimously approved Budget Development Guidelines.

conflicts.issue: Montclair Phase II Boundary: 1,000-Foot Chain-Link Fence vs. 25-Foot Undisturbed Buffer (Item 7)
conflicts.summary: Adjacent property owner Michael Hining urged Council to reject Montclair Phase II unless the developer built a 1,000-foot chain-link fence separating the subdivision from his 12-acre farm, whereas the developer refused the fence and offered a 25-foot undisturbed buffer.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with a 25-foot undisturbed buffer along the shared property line without requiring a chain-link fence.
side_a_arguments: A chain-link fence is ineffective because people can climb over or walk around it, and law enforcement already addresses trespassing.
Requiring fences along every property line with potential foot traffic would set an unworkable precedent across Durham.
A 25-foot undisturbed buffer adds 15 feet beyond the 10-foot code minimum and benefits both the neighbor and new homeowners (Jared Edens for David Weekley Homes).
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning unless the developer installs a chain-link fence along the 1,000-foot boundary.
side_b_arguments: The neighboring 12-acre farm contains ponds and over 50 fruit trees that pose an attractive nuisance and child safety hazard.
Phase II doubles the nearby housing count and number of children, and a 25-foot buffer or no-trespassing signs will not stop children from entering the farm (Michael Hining).
conflicts.resolution: While Council Member Steve Schewel acknowledged struggling with the request, Council accepted the 25-foot undisturbed buffer proffer and approved Montclair Phase II 6-0.

conflicts.issue: Acceptance vs. Mere Receipt of the Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Recommendations (Item 28)
conflicts.summary: Council tied 3-3 on adopting a resolution accepting the Durham Traffic Separation Study recommendations, then voted 6-0 merely to receive the report without endorsing its conceptual street closures.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the staff-recommended resolution accepting the TSS report with caveats requiring future project-specific studies and public input.
side_a_arguments: The resolution explicitly conditioned any implementation on subsequent project-specific studies, public engagement, and City Council approval.
Accepting the final report concluded the study phase while preserving Council veto power over individual rail crossings.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the approval resolution and merely receive the report so conceptual closures like Dillard Street are not treated as adopted city policy.
side_b_arguments: Accepting recommendations lacking broad community support creates an expectation that projects like closing Dillard Street are moving forward.
Durham Area Designers noted the limited scenarios evaluated were conceptual at best and potentially damaging to downtown livability.
conflicts.resolution: The resolution accepting the TSS recommendations failed on a 3-3 tie (Diane Catotti absent), and Steve Schewel's motion merely to receive the report passed 6-0.

conflicts.issue: FY 2014-2015 Budget Guidelines – Scope and Tax Level of Dedicated Parks Funding ('Penny for Parks')
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether dedicated property tax funding for parks should be used for new facilities and land expansion or restricted strictly to maintenance and renovation of existing assets, and weighed tax/fee burdens on lower-income residents before settling on an informational study capped at 1 cent solely for maintenance and renovation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Limit any dedicated parks funding strictly to maintaining and renovating existing parks and trails (no new facilities or land acquisition) and study up to 1 cent alongside peer-city tax/fee and park policing data.
side_a_arguments: Existing parks and recreation facilities face severe deferred maintenance deficiencies that must be addressed before building new facilities or buying land.
Raising taxes without clear maintenance priorities, police protection of park assets, and analysis of cumulative water/sewer/stormwater/solid-waste burdens could hurt low-income residents.
conflicts.side_b_position: Seek new parks facilities in addition to maintenance and renovation (initially championed by Steve Schewel before conceding a 6-1 council majority against new facilities, shifting to a 0.5-cent maintenance/renovation study).
side_b_arguments: A majority of Council still supported exploring dedicated funding for parks and trails maintenance and renovation so Council could review concrete service-level options between 0 and 0.5 cents (or up to 1 cent) during budget workshops.
Underutilized small parks could also be evaluated for repurposing rather than purely selling or abandoning.
conflicts.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel conceded on record that his push for new parks facilities lacked support (6-1) and moved an amended guideline—approved 7-0—directing staff to present a specific plan for parks and trails maintenance and renovation at funding levels not to exceed 1 cent per $100 assessed value.

conflicts.issue: Include Durham County Sheriff's Stolen Firearms Felony Enhancement Proposal in 2015 Long Session Legislative Agenda
conflicts.summary: Senior Assistant to the City Manager Karmisha Wallace explained that the Sheriff requested council support—without requiring city lobbying—to elevate larceny, sale, or receipt of stolen firearms from a Class H to a Class E felony and establish a 72-month mandatory minimum sentence for felonies committed with a stolen firearm. Public speakers Leo Rupert (Carolina Justice Policy Center), Marcia Owen (Religious Coalition for a Nonviolent Durham), and Prof. George Wilson (NCCU) opposed the proposal as counterproductive, arguing it equates property theft with violent crimes against persons, imposes ~$175,000 incarceration costs per sentence without deterrence evidence, and worsens mass incarceration compared to safe-storage education or gun legislation. Sheriff Mike Andrews and legal advisor Curtis Massey arrived mid-debate to argue that rising residential break-ins (30-40% increase, including stolen gun safes) and street gun violence justify Class E classification alongside other hazard offenses, with Mayor Bell, Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden, and Council Member Brown voicing support for sending a strong anti-violence message. However, Council Members Steve Schewel, Don Moffitt, and Eddie Davis criticized the lack of consultation with the NC Sentencing Commission, the absence of crime-reduction projections, and the removal of judicial discretion through a six-year mandatory minimum, and Schewel requested an up-or-down vote on isolating the Sheriff's request, which failed 3-4.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.issue: Police Consent Search Policy, Marijuana Enforcement, and Community Trust (Item 4: City Manager's HRC/CPRB Report)
conflicts.summary: While Council did not vote on Item 4, council members pressed City Manager Tom Bonfield and DPD leadership to go further than the manager's report on mandatory written consent forms for vehicle searches and lowering enforcement priority for low-level marijuana offenses.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require written consent forms for all consensual vehicle searches, deprioritize low-level marijuana arrests, and expand neighborhood foot patrols and informant protections.
side_a_arguments: Young Black men report arbitrary stops, making written consent forms urgent and legally permissible.
High marijuana arrest rates among African American males induct young people into the criminal justice system despite polling favoring treatment.
McDougald Terrace residents want officers out of patrol cars walking neighborhoods and stronger confidentiality when reporting crimes.
conflicts.side_b_position: City Manager's report favored officer discretion on vehicle consent searches (requiring written/recorded consent for homes and HEAT teams), semi-annual data reviews, and multi-agency dialogue before changing marijuana enforcement.
side_b_arguments: Requiring written forms during every patrol traffic stop raises situational control and officer safety considerations.
Meaningful changes to low-level drug enforcement require buy-in from the District Attorney, Sheriff, and District Court judges.
DPD has already begun Fair and Impartial Policing racial equity training and expanded data analytics.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; City Manager Bonfield committed to returning for a comprehensive page-by-page work-session discussion on Thursday, September 4, 2014.

conflicts.issue: Length and Scope of Downtown Resident Parking Fee Phase-Out (Item 5)
conflicts.summary: Downtown residents, council members, and the City Attorney debated whether early downtown residents could retain free or discounted parking, how long a half-rate phase-in should last, and whether post-2008 residents could be excluded.
conflicts.side_a_position: Provide an extended multi-year half-price phase-in for current downtown residents (Don Moffitt initially favored 10 years, plus surface-lot rate relief; Coke Ariail/Kate Dobbs sought preservation of free parking).
side_a_arguments: Early downtown homeowners bought properties relying on city promises of free parking and helped revitalize downtown and grow property tax receipts (William 'Coke' Ariail, Kate Dobbs).

Charging full rates immediately asks ~130 downtown residents—who already pay higher downtown tax rates—for an extra $100,000/year, and Main Street residents prefer surface parking for safety (Don Moffitt).
conflicts.side_b_position: Limit subsidies to pre-2008 'pioneer' residents if legally possible, or keep the phase-out brief to avoid larger revenue losses.
side_b_arguments: Residents moving in after 2008 were aware of changing policies and should not receive the same long-term subsidy as the ~21 original pioneers (Steve Schewel).
Extending the 50% discount beyond three years costs the city approximately $50,000 in foregone revenue per additional year (clarified by Diane Catotti).
Legally, a retroactive 2008 cutoff would be arbitrary and capricious, leaving a uniform phase-out for all current residents as the only defensible option (City Attorney).
conflicts.resolution: Council compromised 6-0 on Don Moffitt's motion, seconded by Steve Schewel, adopting Option 2 with a five-year half-price phase-in for all current downtown residents through December 31, 2018.

conflicts.issue: Police Transparency, Racial Disparities in Traffic Stops, and Critical Incident Disclosures
conflicts.summary: During the third-quarter crime report, council members and residents debated how aggressively the Durham Police Department should release information and address racial profiling concerns amid pending SBI investigations.
conflicts.side_a_position: Demand faster public disclosure of critical incident facts and non-defensive reform of traffic-stop and policing practices.
side_a_arguments: Public confidence in police truthfulness and transparency requires timely answers on the Jesus Huerta, Derek Walker, and Jose Ocampo cases rather than months-long waits.
FADE's traffic-stop and search disparity statistics require open-minded review and concrete reforms.
Community activist Victoria Peterson called for replacing the Police Chief over homicides, lawsuits, and mental health crisis handling.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defend the Police Department's record while respecting independent SBI, Medical Examiner, and District Attorney investigative processes.
side_b_arguments: Part 1 crime is at a 14-year low and the vast majority of officers serve fairly without bias.
Underfunding of the SBI crime lab and Chief Medical Examiner delays limit what factual information the city can legally and ethically release before investigations conclude.
Chief Lopez urged community members to come forward with information on street violence rather than waiting solely on police.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote; council members expressed support for ongoing Human Relations Commission hearings and police internal review reforms while awaiting SBI findings.

conflicts.issue: Process and Transit Scoring Criteria for Dedicated Housing Funding Guidelines (Item 4)
conflicts.summary: Community member Stephen Hopkins and Mayor Bell objected to adopting new small-project and neighborhood revitalization scoring criteria without external public review, while Schewel requested adding half-mile transit-station bonus points.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue adoption for two weeks to October 23 work session so staff can incorporate transit-proximity bonus points and solicit public comments.
side_a_arguments: No external housing stakeholders had reviewed the draft scoring criteria prior to the Council vote.
Incorporating Bo Glenn's last-minute suggestion for 4 bonus points near light rail stations warrants transparent public circulation via listserv.
A brief two-week delay will not derail late-December or early-January application timelines.
conflicts.side_b_position: Original staff recommendation sought immediate adoption to issue competitive application documents without delay before Assistant Director Larry Jarvis's departure.
side_b_arguments: Adopting guidelines promptly gives prospective developers adequate optioning and due diligence time ahead of late December/early January deadlines.
Staff followed the same internal drafting process used in prior funding cycles.
conflicts.resolution: Continued 6-0 to the October 23 work session with direction to add 4 transit-proximity bonus points and circulate the draft for public feedback.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 21, 2014
conflicts.issue: Written Consent for Vehicle Searches, Camera Mandates, CPRB Authority, and Marijuana Enforcement (HRC/CPRB Response)
conflicts.summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield's 131-page response and supporters (including FOP lodges and Hispanic community speakers) backed discretionary patrol vehicle consent searches and a measured review of DPD practices, whereas Council Members Steve Schewel and Cora Cole-McFadden and FADE/People's Alliance/NAACP/Durham CAN speakers demanded mandatory written vehicle search consent, stricter camera rules, independent CPRB authority, and immediate action on racial disparities.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require mandatory written consent forms for all vehicle consent searches, establish firmer camera activation rules, and pursue marijuana deprioritization and stronger civilian oversight.
side_a_arguments: Written consent is the most reliable safeguard against racial disparities in vehicle stops where dashcams/microphones cannot capture out-of-range encounters.
Wait-and-see data reviews until 2015 fail to stop ongoing harm, including 86% of simple marijuana arrests falling on African Americans.

Advocacy groups (FADE, SCSJ, People's Alliance, Durham CAN, NAACP, Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People) warned that without mandatory written vehicle consent and CPRB investigative authority, systemic disparities will persist.
conflicts.side_b_position: Adopt the City Manager's recommendations requiring written/recorded consent only for home/premises and HEAT-team searches while preserving patrol officer discretion, and defend Chief Jose Lopez and DPD.
side_b_arguments: Requiring patrol officers to return to cruisers for paper forms during traffic stops creates officer safety and situational control risks.
DPD has already launched Fair and Impartial Policing training, expanded CIT training (180 officers), and strong data analytics.
Police union (FOP Lodge #2) and Hispanic speakers urged adopting Bonfield's report and opposed calls to remove Chief Lopez.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote on the substance at the work session; Item 4 was placed on the September 2 General Business Agenda for Council deliberation.

conflicts.issue: Delaying vs. Enacting Revisions to the Roadside Solicitation (Panhandling) Ordinance (Item 3)
conflicts.summary: Public speakers and council members differed over whether to refer the revised roadside solicitation ordinance back to work session for additional residential-protection rules or enact it after a year of deliberation, as well as over the city's broader approach to panhandling.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move forward promptly with the consensus ordinance revision and allow regulated solicitation so impoverished residents are not further harmed by delays.
side_a_arguments: Stakeholders, police, the city attorney's office, and the Homeless Services Advisory Committee subcommittee spent over a year developing an alternative and reaching consensus.
Repeated postponements prolong hardship for individuals who rely on begging for sustenance (Carolyn Schul).
conflicts.side_b_position: Refer the ordinance back to work session to add residential protections and address ongoing neighborhood and business impacts rather than continuing to permit street begging.
side_b_arguments: Technical adjustments for driver-side solicitation on one-way streets were still unfinished, and Springfield, Missouri's rules protecting residents living near parks and intersections needed review (Bill Bell).
Large clusters of panhandlers along Fayetteville Street, Roxboro Road, and Alston Avenue hurt African-American business districts (Victoria Peterson).
Permitting solicitation fails to transform lives or end panhandling, and the city should pursue different strategies to connect people with resources (Cora Cole-McFadden).
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 6-0 to refer Item 3 to the Thursday work session for further review.

conflicts.issue: Downtown Residential Parking Pass Rate Increases and Grandfathering
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over how to transition roughly 128-130 existing downtown residents onto higher parking garage rates after the City Attorney advised that permanent grandfathering distinguishing existing from future residents was not legally permissible.
conflicts.side_a_position: Protect existing downtown residents through extended relief, a five-year fixed-rate pass option, or honoring historical commitments
side_a_arguments: Since the 1980s, Durham's downtown revitalization depended on attracting residents downtown through supportive parking policies
Abruptly raising rates on existing residents breaks prior expectations and hurts public trust
A five-year fixed-rate pass available to anyone for 30 days could provide relief without illegal permanent grandfathering
conflicts.side_b_position: Question legal/administrative complexity of special pass carve-outs and evaluate uniform phase-in or revenue-neutral options
side_b_arguments: City Attorney advised the city cannot legally distinguish between existing and future downtown residents
Staff's two-to-three-year phase-in option generates less revenue initially while avoiding legal vulnerability
Council should know the actual dollar impact before adopting a special five-year pass mechanism that could face legal challenge
conflicts.resolution: No final vote was taken; Council requested staff fiscal impact analysis and legal review of the five-year pass concept while considering extending the January 1 deferral temporarily.

conflicts.issue: Wexford Science & Technology (Chesterfield Building) $6M Incentive and County Contribution Share
conflicts.summary: Council members debated the fiscal return of the city's $6 million, 15-year incentive for Wexford Science & Technology's adaptive reuse of the Chesterfield Building and whether Durham County's $2.6 million contribution was adequate.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support the city incentive as a necessary partnership with the county to rescue and activate the deteriorating Chesterfield Building.
side_a_arguments: Adaptive reuse of the former factory into lab space is cost-prohibitive after multiple failed redevelopment attempts.
Durham County carries a much larger budget and school funding mandates and is not obligated to contribute, yet its $2.6 million makes the deal viable.
Without the agreement, the Chesterfield Building will remain an eyesore and continue to deteriorate, whereas completion generates long-term net revenues.
conflicts.side_b_position: Question the city's fiscal exposure and criticize Durham County's $2.6 million commitment as disproportionately small.
side_b_arguments: The county's $2.6 million contribution over five years is inadequate relative to the city's $6 million over 15 years and the parking deck arrangements.
The fiscal and tax return structure requires stricter scrutiny before committing millions in city incentives.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed (exact numeric tally not stated in the transcript excerpt).

conflicts.issue: Substitute-to-the-Substitute Motion: Proceed with NCDOT Resurfacing of Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard and Defer Striping Decision
conflicts.summary: Following business-owner opposition to reducing Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard from five lanes to three lanes, council first moved to delay for one two-week cycle, then voted 5-2 on a substitute motion by Don Moffitt to approve staff's 3-lane restriping plan before reopening that vote for procedural clarification. Council Member Eugene Brown then moved a substitute-to-the-substitute to accept NCDOT-funded resurfacing immediately and return by late June to decide the striping configuration; staff noted NCDOT would revert to existing 5-lane striping if council did not decide within six weeks, and the motion passed 4-3 with Diane Catotti, Don Moffitt, and Steve Schewel voting no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 10D (Severed): Substitute Motion Option 1 — Repeal $1.80/Month Solid Waste Fee & Adopt Commercial/Yard Waste Fee Schedules
conflicts.summary: At Mayor Bell's request, Item 10D was severed from the FY 2014-15 budget for an intense policy debate. Council Member Steve Schewel moved Option 1 to repeal the $1.80/month ($21.60/year) solid waste collection fee and replace its ~$1.4 million revenue with property taxes, joined by Diane Catotti and Don Moffitt, who argued the flat fee was regressive (hurting homeowners below ~$370,000 and renters who pay $0 directly under property tax) and would require a 56% hike next year to cover an $800,000 projected shortfall. Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden, Mayor Bill Bell, and Council Member Eugene Brown opposed repeal, arguing the solid waste enterprise fund already received $9.6 million in property tax subsidies, user fees akin to DATA bus fares were sound business practice, low-income residents had not complained, and adding ~0.6 cents to the tax rate risked giving Durham the highest municipal property tax rate in North Carolina. The substitute motion passed 4-3, with Bell, Brown, and Cole-McFadden voting no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Excluding Wide Utility Easements from Tree Coverage Calculations (TC1300002)
conflicts.summary: Council and public speakers divided sharply over Horvath Associates' proposal to exclude utility easements of 50 feet or wider from tree-coverage calculations while still counting those easements toward residential density and impervious-surface allowances.
conflicts.side_a_position: Exclude wide utility easements (minus the first 50 feet) from gross tract area when calculating required tree coverage.
side_a_arguments: Power companies prohibit tree planting in wide transmission easements, forcing developers to set aside extra buildable acreage (e.g., 7.5 acres at Del Webb Carolina Arbors) to meet tree-coverage minimums.
Existing UDO exemptions already exclude ponds and road-widening rights-of-way where trees cannot be planted.
Preserving usable acreage lowers site development costs and improves housing affordability (Ron Horvath, Jared Edens, George Stancil).
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject or restrict the universal easement exemption so tree canopy is not reduced on large developments or near sensitive watersheds without parcel-level analysis.
side_b_arguments: Developers continue to receive full density and impervious-surface credit from the easement while shedding the corresponding tree-coverage obligation, harming air quality and raising urban temperatures (Will Wilson, Steve Schewel).
Staff had not mapped affected parcels near protected watersheds such as New Hope Creek, Ellerbe Creek, and the Eno River (Bob Healy, Pat Carstensen).
While small tracts encumbered by wide power easements might merit relief, there is no clear public interest in reducing tree requirements for very large developments (Steve Schewel).
conflicts.resolution: Unable to support the text amendment as drafted, Council voted 7-0 to reopen and continue the public hearing to May 19, 2014 so staff and the applicant could map affected parcels and model tract-size or percentage thresholds.

conflicts.issue: Continuum of Care / Homeless Funding Scoring Fairness and Transparency (Item 15)
conflicts.summary: During the Annual Action Plan public hearing, nonprofit leader Sharon Elliott-Bynum challenged the fairness and transparency of Community Development's Continuum of Care funding recommendations, prompting Council scrutiny despite staff explaining it was a separate process from CDBG/HOME/ESG.
conflicts.side_a_position: Investigate and reform funding recommendations to ensure fair scoring, process clarity, and inclusion of smaller/new nonprofits such as female veterans housing.
side_a_arguments: CAARE Inc.'s proposal to rehab a home for four homeless female veterans scored an average of 85 from the Citizens Advisory Committee compared to 84 for the staff-recommended agency, yet was passed over (Sharon Elliott-Bynum).
The recommended project was part two of a renewal rather than a new project, and an earlier $28,000 award from 2008-09 was never disbursed after the prior director's death (Sharon Elliott-Bynum).

Council must fully investigate the process at Thursday's work session because having the same organizations receive funding repeatedly does not appear fair (Cora Cole-McFadden; follow-up also requested by Bill Bell).
conflicts.side_b_position: Clarify that Continuum of Care recommendations follow a separate HUD process overseen by the Homeless Services Advisory Committee rather than the CDBG/HOME/ESG Annual Action Plan.
side_b_arguments: The funding cited by Ms. Bynum comes from the Continuum of Care process scheduled before the Homeless Services Advisory Committee, which makes recommendations separately from the Annual Action Plan hearing (Community Development Director Reginald Johnson).
Staff would research the historical $28,000 award question separately.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 7-0 to receive all public hearing comments while directing Community Development staff to investigate Ms. Bynum's complaints and report back at Thursday's work session.

conflicts.issue: Conducting a Joint City-County Resident Survey
conflicts.summary: Mayor Bill Bell questioned the value of combining city and county service questions into a single joint resident survey, while another Council member defended staff's rationale that a joint survey strengthened the community assessment.
conflicts.side_a_position: Limit the city resident survey to city residents and city services rather than combining with county questions.
side_a_arguments: Asking residents outside city limits or across jurisdictions about both county and city operations (such as sheriff protection vs. city services) creates confusion.
The survey is already long and gains little value from mixing distinct city and county responsibilities.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support staff's joint city-county community survey approach.
side_b_arguments: Staff (Josh Edwards) made a strong case that surveying the broader community strengthens the survey and works well across both governments.
conflicts.resolution: Discussion concluded without altering the survey or taking a separate vote.

conflicts.issue: Income Targeting for Downtown and Transit-Oriented Rent Subsidies
conflicts.summary: During review of the Enterprise Community Partners affordable housing consulting contract (Item 6), Mayor Bill Bell and Council colleagues differed over whether direct local rent subsidies should target 60%-80% AMI working households or deeper affordability below 50%-60% AMI.
conflicts.side_a_position: Create a shallow rent subsidy tool targeting 60%-80% AMI working families near downtown and transit stations, aligned with Council's TOD resolution.
side_a_arguments: Council previously adopted a transit-oriented development resolution specifically targeting 60%-80% AMI families within a half-mile of transit stops.
Downtown apartments under construction are unaffordable at market rates to working people in the 60%-80% AMI band without a shallow subsidy tool.
conflicts.side_b_position: Prioritize direct rent subsidies for households with the greatest need (under 50%-60% AMI) and await the consultant's citywide study before selecting operational tactics.
side_b_arguments: If the city directly subsidizes rent, scarce funds should serve households under 50% or 60% AMI rather than 60%-80% AMI.
Debating specific subsidy tactics is premature until Enterprise Community Partners completes its assessment of needs and tools.
conflicts.resolution: Item 6 was placed on the General Business Agenda for further consideration while Enterprise Community Partners began its study.

conflicts.issue: Police Officer Staffing Request Logic vs. Long-Term Crime Decline (2014 Annual Crime Report)
conflicts.summary: During discussion of the 2014 Annual Crime Report, Council Member Steve Schewel disputed Police Chief Jose Lopez's budget rationale for adding frontline police officers based on a one-year spike in aggravated assaults, while public speaker Victoria Peterson clashed with Mayor Bill Bell over Council responsiveness to Black homicide victims.
conflicts.side_a_position: A 15% one-year rise in Part 1 violent crime (driven by aggravated assaults and shootings into residences/vehicles) requires additional police staffing and targeted enforcement.
side_a_arguments: Shooting into occupied dwellings and vehicles increased aggravated assault victim counts by 23% in 2014.
Police leadership argued in budget sessions that additional line officers are needed to address violent crime and improve response-time targets.
conflicts.side_b_position: A single-year spike in aggravated assaults does not logically justify permanent officer increases given a 15-year 40% crime decline; any expansion must be justified by specific community-policing plans.
side_b_arguments: Durham achieved a 40% long-term drop in crime since 2000 and near-record-low property crime with roughly the same or fewer officers.

Four different departmental staffing formulas yielded estimates ranging from zero to 111 added officers, showing the department needs to present a concrete community-policing model before expecting Council budget support.
conflicts.resolution: Informational report (no vote); Chief Lopez agreed to keep Schewel's community-policing criteria in mind during upcoming budget deliberations.

conflicts.issue: Durham Station / Jackson Street Excess Land RFP Housing Ratio and Flexibility
conflicts.summary: Council members split over whether the Durham Station / Jackson Street RFP should invite flexible market-rate and mixed-income proposals pending the February affordable housing consultant report or mandate an 80% affordable / 20% market-rate housing ratio.
conflicts.side_a_position: Keep all three RFP options open—including mixed-income and market-rate options—and avoid arbitrary ratios before receiving the February affordable housing consultant report.
side_a_arguments: Setting strict income breakdowns (e.g., 30%/60%/80% AMI) prematurely without financing data would be arbitrary.
An open RFP lets developers show feasible financing stacks and wait for the consultant's recommendations before Council evaluates proposals.
conflicts.side_b_position: Commit to an 80% affordable / 20% market-rate target and prioritize maximizing affordable housing units without office space.
side_b_arguments: Prior direction sought to skew heavily toward low- and moderate-income housing with no more than 20% market-rate units.
Following through on the 80/20 commitment avoids drifting away from affordable housing goals.
conflicts.resolution: Staff noted Council could weight scoring points toward desired housing ratios and requested Council direction before finalizing the RFP.

conflicts.issue: Local Historic Landmark Designation: Wiley and Elizabeth Forbes House (LD150002)
conflicts.summary: Pat Young presented the local historic landmark designation for 3307 Devon Road (one of the first 20 structures in Hope Valley), supplemented by a newly added fiscal impact analysis. After the clerk initially misread the tally as 6-1, she corrected the official result to 5-2 with Eugene Brown and Diane Catotti voting no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 5-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (5-2)

conflicts.issue: Police Headquarters Site Design and Retention of Carpenter Chevrolet Building
conflicts.summary: Council and design stakeholders weighed whether to adopt Schemes 4 or 5—removing the Carpenter Chevrolet building and pulling the Police Headquarters to Main Street—or pursue the Durham Area Designers (DAD) proposal retaining Carpenter Chevrolet for future private development.
conflicts.side_a_position: Proceed with Scheme 4 or Scheme 5 without retaining Carpenter Chevrolet.
side_a_arguments: Avoids roughly $1.8 million to $2 million in site-compression and additional capital costs.
Retains full city design control along Main Street rather than relying on uncertain future private development.
conflicts.side_b_position: Preserve the Carpenter Chevrolet building and enable adjacent private development per the DAD concept.
side_b_arguments: Preserves the historic Carpenter Chevrolet structure while creating future private development opportunities on the parcel.
Addresses concerns about police headquarters buildings appearing as glassless fortresses.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; staff requested Council's preferred site layout by October 8 to advance to schematic design.

conflicts.issue: Carpenter Chevrolet Building Preservation at New Police Headquarters Site
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to spend an estimated $4 million to preserve the historic Carpenter Chevrolet building as part of the new police headquarters design along Fayetteville/Main Street, weighing historic preservation against capital budget constraints and street-level activation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Oppose spending $4 million to preserve the Carpenter Chevrolet building
side_a_arguments: Spending $4 million on the structure was not justified relative to the building's assessed value and other capital needs.
No private developer had ever offered to purchase the building alone prior to city acquisition.
conflicts.side_b_position: Explore cost-effective preservation or active pedestrian-oriented alternatives
side_b_arguments: Historical context helps define Durham's identity rather than 'anywhere USA,' and at least one developer had expressed prior interest in the site.
Any preserved or redeveloped frontage should provide active uses residents want to walk to, rather than blank landscaping, if achievable without a $4 million cost.
conflicts.resolution: Deferred by consensus for apples-to-apples staff comparison at the September 24 or first October work session

conflicts.issue: Zoning Map Change: US 70 Self Storage Center (Z1400020)
conflicts.summary: Pat Young presented Z1400020 to rezone 7.55 acres on US 70 to IL(D) for a self-storage center despite a 1-10 denial recommendation from the Planning Commission. After the applicant added a commitment to record a permanent access easement prior to building permit or certificate of occupancy, Council Member Don Moffitt seconded the approval motion and voiced reluctant support, and Council passed the rezoning 5-2 with Diane Catotti and Eddie Davis voting no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 5-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (5-2)

conflicts.issue: Expedited RFP Timeline for 9% LIHTC Affordable Housing Near Durham Station
conflicts.summary: Council members differed over whether to put an expedited Durham Station land RFP on the September 8 action agenda to meet the January 9% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) application deadline or allow more time for public discussion and consultant input.
conflicts.side_a_position: Place an expedited RFP item on the September 8 agenda so qualified affordable housing applicants can compete for January 9% tax credits.
side_a_arguments: 9% LIHTC funding is highly valuable and requires site control/selection before the early January deadline.
Durham Housing Authority, Self-Help Credit Union, and private developers have expressed interest in building affordable housing near Durham Station.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid rushing a major land-disposition policy decision before full public discussion and the affordable housing consultant's work.
side_b_arguments: Council has not yet held a full public discussion on site priorities, ownership mechanics, and potential local dollar commitments.
Rushing a single strategy contradicts waiting for the affordable housing consultant to evaluate citywide tools.
conflicts.resolution: Rather than placing the item on the September 8 regular agenda, Council agreed without a formal vote to schedule it for the September 10 work session.

conflicts.issue: Enterprise Community Partners Affordable Housing Consulting Timeline and Income Targeting (Item 6)
conflicts.summary: Council members debated the $201,000 Phase 1 consulting contract with Enterprise Community Partners, Inc., clashing over whether a five-month delivery timeline was overly complex and whether housing subsidies should target 60–80% AMI or focus strictly under 60% AMI.
conflicts.side_a_position: Shorten timeline to 90 days and avoid overcomplicating program design
side_a_arguments: The five-month timeline is unrealistic and overthinks a program design that should be delivered within 90 days.
