meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Presided over by Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden (with Mayor Bill Bell excused), the Durham City Council debated an accelerated affordable housing RFP near Durham Station, reviewed advisory board attendance rules, and examined Police Headquarters capital shortfalls. A proposal to add an item to the September 8 meeting directing an expedited RFP for 9% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) development near Durham Station drew pushback from members concerned about rushing public land disposition without full public discussion, and was instead scheduled for the September 10 work session. Council unanimously passed a motion directing the City Clerk to bring forward policy options on boards and commissions attendance (Item 5), reviewed the draft 2015 Resident Survey (Item 6), deferred any decision on retaining the Carpenter Chevrolet building amid Police Headquarters/911 budget gaps ($18.5M unadjusted gap), and unanimously approved priority items, the September 8 agenda, and a closed session.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Expedited 9% LIHTC Affordable Housing RFP Near Durham Station
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A member proposed placing an item on the September 8 agenda directing staff to design an expedited RFP for excess land near Durham Station—noting interest from the Durham Housing Authority, Self-Help Credit Union, and private developers—to meet the January 9% tax credit deadline. In extended discussion at 02:45:01, other members objected to rushing a major land policy decision without full public vetting; Council agreed without a motion to place the topic on the September 10 work session.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items (Resident Survey, Paving STT-74 & Herndon/Barbee Roundabout)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items covering the 2015 Resident Survey presentation (Item 6), a request to suspend rules to vote on the 2015 street repair and repaving contract STT-74 (Item 13), and supplemental Item 17 supporting discretionary state legislative funding for a roundabout at Herndon and Barbee Roads.

agenda_items.title: Transit Driver Retirements, Consent Review & Board Attendance Policy Motion (Item 5)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council recognized retiring transit drivers Ron and Gail and reviewed Consent Items 1-12, including Google Fiber North Carolina LLC network hut licensing (Item 11) and an NCSU agreement (Item 7). On Item 5 (Boards, Committees, and Commissions Attendance Reports for FY 2014-15), Council unanimously passed a motion directing the City Clerk to prepare an agenda item reviewing attendance policies alongside interlocal-agreement constraints and demographic breakdowns.

agenda_items.title: 2015 Resident Survey Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson and Strategic Initiatives Manager Josh Edwards presented the draft 2015 Resident Survey for Council feedback prior to distribution. Council Member Eddie Davis commented on whether survey respondents distinguish between city and county responsibilities.

agenda_items.title: Police Headquarters / 911 Facility Capital Gap & Carpenter Building Options
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented 10-year capital model projections for the new Police Headquarters and 911 facility, showing an $18.5M gap before incorporating an estimated $3M+ county 911 share, $9.6M in preferred program cost reductions, and $7.2M-$7.8M in potential property sales. Council discussed whether retaining the Carpenter Chevrolet building (~$2M added cost) was feasible and deferred a decision with several members absent.

agenda_items.title: Setting the September 8 Agenda, Appointment Ballots & Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously set the September 8 regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 1-12; GBA Item 14; GBA Public Hearing Item 15; Disposed Item 13) and reported ballot results (Citizens Advisory Committee had no 4-vote majority and moved to GBA with Barry Botch at 3 votes; Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Commission filled with 5 votes). Council then voted unanimously to enter closed session.

votes.item_title: City Manager Priority Items (Item 6, Item 13 STT-74 Paving, Supplemental Item 17 Herndon/Barbee Roundabout)
votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell had an excused absence; five votes were recorded on appointment ballots at 02:59:36 (individual roll-call calls for the remaining seats were garbled in ASR, with Eddie Davis confirmed speaking at 00:30:19).
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted the City Manager's priority items as outlined.

votes.item_title: Direct City Clerk to Prepare Agenda Item on Board & Commission Attendance Policies (Item 5)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously by voice vote with Bill Bell excused.
votes.discussion_detail: Directed the City Clerk to prepare an agenda item reviewing how to update attendance policies for city boards and commissions, including interlocal constraints and county policy comparisons.

votes.item_title: Setting the September 8 Regular Council Meeting Agenda (Consent 1-12; GBA 14; Public Hearing 15; Disposed 13)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously by voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the September 8 meeting agenda with Consent Items 1-12, GBA Item 14, Public Hearing Item 15, and Item 13 disposed (and CAC appointment moved to GBA after ballots).

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session
votes.notes: Passed unanimously by voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Entered closed session for the stated reason.

disagreements.issue: Expedited RFP Timeline for 9% LIHTC Affordable Housing Near Durham Station
disagreements.summary: Council members differed over whether to put an expedited Durham Station land RFP on the September 8 action agenda to meet the January 9% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) application deadline or allow more time for public discussion and consultant input.
disagreements.side_a_position: Place an expedited RFP item on the September 8 agenda so qualified affordable housing applicants can compete for January 9% tax credits.
side_a_arguments: 9% LIHTC funding is highly valuable and requires site control/selection before the early January deadline.
Durham Housing Authority, Self-Help Credit Union, and private developers have expressed interest in building affordable housing near Durham Station.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid rushing a major land-disposition policy decision before full public discussion and the affordable housing consultant's work.
side_b_arguments: Council has not yet held a full public discussion on site priorities, ownership mechanics, and potential local dollar commitments.
Rushing a single strategy contradicts waiting for the affordable housing consultant to evaluate citywide tools.
disagreements.resolution: Rather than placing the item on the September 8 regular agenda, Council agreed without a formal vote to schedule it for the September 10 work session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council August 17, 2015
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, the Durham City Council added a resolution opposing state redistribution of local sales tax as priority Item 24 (7-0) and unanimously approved the consent agenda (7-0), including a five-year City-County inspections interlocal renewal, Morreene Road Apartments financing approval, three bicycle/pedestrian grant agreements, a 3810 Page Road condemnation for the Southeast Pressure Zone, and towing fee revisions. Council debated Item 6, a $201,000 Phase 1 consulting contract with Enterprise Community Partners, Inc. to design an affordable housing strategy—clashing over its five-month timeline versus 90 days and targeting 60–80% AMI versus under 60% AMI—before an omitted transcript gap. Council subsequently passed an unidentified planning item (7-0), adopted preliminary and final resolutions ordering street completions in Ravenstone and Stonehill Estates (7-0) with 10-year, zero-interest assessments averaging $22.51 and $21.09 monthly, passed Item 24 opposing sales tax redistribution (7-0), and approved two excused absence requests (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Priority Item 24 Addition and Consent Agenda Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield requested adding supplemental Item 24 (a resolution opposing local sales tax redistribution) as a priority item, which Council approved 7-0. Council then unanimously adopted the consent agenda (7-0), covering the June 2015 Grants Management audit, a five-year City-County inspections interlocal agreement renewal, Housing Authority financing approval for Morreene Road Apartments, bike/pedestrian grant agreements on Carpenter Fletcher, Cornwallis, and Hillandale Roads, a 3810 Page Road utility condemnation, workforce grant amendments, and towing fee revisions.

agenda_items.title: Consulting Contract with Enterprise Community Partners, Inc. ($201,000)

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Presided over by Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden with Mayor Bill Bell present, the Durham City Council approved a roadside memorials policy review, heard concerns over transit contractor benefits, and debated downtown affordable housing subsidy targets. Council unanimously passed a motion directing staff to consider alternatives to the current memorials policy, which allowed a single citizen's complaint to trigger removal. During Citizens Matters, speakers raised concerns about PAC storage and youth access at Holton Career and Resource Center, as well as seniority and retirement benefits for contracted transit workers transitioning from Linear Monarch to Republic. On Item 6 (Enterprise Community Partners affordable housing consulting), Mayor Bell argued for developing a shallow rent subsidy for working families at 60%-80% AMI near downtown transit stops, whereas another council member argued direct rent subsidies should target lower-income households (under 50%-60% AMI). Council closed by unanimously setting the regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roadside Memorials Policy Review Motion

agenda_items.title: Enterprise Community Partners Contract & Transit-Oriented Housing Subsidy Policy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: During discussion of the Enterprise Community Partners engagement, Mayor Bill Bell cited Council's transit-oriented development resolution targeting 60%-80% AMI households within a half-mile of transit stops and urged creating a shallow rent subsidy tool for working families priced out of downtown apartments. Another Council member countered that direct rent subsidies should serve lower-income households (under 50%-60% AMI), while a third member advised waiting for the consultant's analysis before choosing specific tactics.

disagreements.issue: Income Targeting for Downtown and Transit-Oriented Rent Subsidies
disagreements.summary: During review of the Enterprise Community Partners affordable housing consulting contract (Item 6), Mayor Bill Bell and Council colleagues differed over whether direct local rent subsidies should target 60%-80% AMI working households or deeper affordability below 50%-60% AMI.
disagreements.side_a_position: Create a shallow rent subsidy tool targeting 60%-80% AMI working families near downtown and transit stations, aligned with Council's TOD resolution.
side_a_arguments: Council previously adopted a transit-oriented development resolution specifically targeting 60%-80% AMI families within a half-mile of transit stops.
Downtown apartments under construction are unaffordable at market rates to working people in the 60%-80% AMI band without a shallow subsidy tool.
disagreements.side_b_position: Prioritize direct rent subsidies for households with the greatest need (under 50%-60% AMI) and await the consultant's citywide study before selecting operational tactics.
side_b_arguments: If the city directly subsidizes rent, scarce funds should serve households under 50% or 60% AMI rather than 60%-80% AMI.
Debating specific subsidy tactics is premature until Enterprise Community Partners completes its assessment of needs and tools.
disagreements.resolution: Item 6 was placed on the General Business Agenda for further consideration while Enterprise Community Partners began its study.

meetings.title: Durham City Council August 3, 2015
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council opened its August 3, 2015 meeting with a National Night Out proclamation and addressed complaints from unpaid workers on the incentivized Residence Inn project at the Old McPherson Hospital site, with staff and the City Attorney explaining that the dispute lay with a subcontractor and required formal contract or mechanic's-lien resolution rather than city mediation. Council unanimously voted 7-0 to accept the City Clerk's priority item invalidating a protest petition on Item 39 after a signature withdrawal, and unanimously passed 7-0 a Unified Development Ordinance text amendment clarifying permissible-by-right encroachments in 10-foot riparian buffer setbacks and updating lot-of-record references to include Wake and Orange counties. Council also held a public hearing on raising the Private Drainage Assistance Program cap from $20,000 to $25,000 and debated Mayor Bill Bell's proposal to accelerate a downtown and transit-corridor affordable housing rental assistance program targeting 60% to 80% AMI households alongside hiring an affordable housing consultant.

agenda_items.title: National Night Out Proclamation

agenda_items.title: Unpaid Subcontractor Dispute on Residence Inn (Old McPherson Hospital) Project

City Manager Tom Bonfield and City Attorney Patrick Baker reported that the Office of Economic and Workforce Development investigated and determined the nonpayment dispute involves a subcontractor, advising affected workers to pursue formal contract dispute resolution, mechanic's liens, or the Department of Labor since the city lacks privity of contract.

agenda_items.title: Mayor Bell's Downtown/Transit Affordable Housing Proposal and Youth Recognition Event
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell previewed a proposal he emailed to council, the City Manager, and the City Attorney for a downtown and half-mile transit-stop rental assistance program for low-to-moderate income families, noting it would be discussed under staff's incentive item and at the Thursday work session. agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented two minor UDO amendments: allowing encroachments already permissible by right under state law and the UDO within the 10-foot riparian buffer no-build setback without requiring Board of Adjustment variances, and expanding the definition of 'lot of record' beyond Durham County to reference Wake and Orange County Register of Deeds offices. meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Presided over by Mayor Bill Bell, the Durham City Council reviewed its consent and public hearing agendas, a five-year police traffic stop data analysis, and cost-recovery options for underground utility locate demands driven by fiber-optic expansion. Council members praised departing Council Member Eugene Brown following his retirement decision and heard public remarks criticizing state legislative preemption of local authority. During the traffic stop review, Council welcomed Durham's lower overall per-capita stop rate compared with peer cities while raising concern over consent search rates remaining roughly 2.5 times higher for African American motorists than White motorists and inquiring about upcoming reporting on low-level marijuana enforcement. On underground utilities, staff estimated $3.4 million in two-year locate and permitting costs tied largely to Google Fiber and AT&T, with Council signaling preference for recovering 100 percent of costs through utility fees rather than tax dollars. Council unanimously approved referring back Item 42 (2014 Evaluation and Assessment Report), confirmed 7-0 board appointment votes for four commissions (alongside a 4-vote appointment to the Passenger Vehicle for Hire Commission), and set the regular meeting agenda unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: City Manager & City Attorney Priority Items (Item 42 Referral & Item 39 Protest Petition)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager requested referring Item 42 (the 2014 Evaluation and Assessment Report, A15-00001) back to the administration so the City-County Planning Department could resubmit it in the next cycle, which Council approved unanimously. The City Attorney informed Council that a protest petition had been filed against Item 39 (Bell Green Road zoning map change, Z14-00026) and was still being evaluated for validity.

agenda_items.title: Consent & Public Hearing Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed consent items including board and commission appointments (Items 2-8), the May 2015 bid report (Item 19), a lease for the Museum of Durham History at 521 West Morgan Street (Item 23), temporary staffing (Item 24), paving equipment rental and driveway/right-of-way ordinance revisions (Items 26-28), and software and telecom contracts (Items 29-31). Public hearing items included zoning map changes on Vessel Avenue, Garrett Road, and Bell Green Road (Items 36-39) and Unified Development Ordinance text amendments on affordable housing parking/density bonuses (TC15-00003) and riparian buffer setbacks (TC15-00004).

agenda_items.title: Citizens Matters & Local Historic District / State Preemption Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers and Council members recognized Council Member Eugene Brown's service following his announcement that he would not seek re-election, noted rising child poverty statistics, and criticized state legislative restrictions on local control over public monuments and procurement. A speaker also questioned staff on local historic design guidelines, the Holloway Street historic district expansion, and Golden Belt.

agenda_items.title: Five-Year Traffic Stop Data Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council and Police Department leadership reviewed five-year traffic stop and search statistics, noting Durham's per-capita stop rate was lower than peer North Carolina cities while search rates stood at 2 percent for White motorists and 8 percent for Black motorists. Council members voiced concern that consent searches remained roughly 2.5 times higher for African Americans than Whites and asked for a September update on low-level marijuana initiatives and clearer differentiation between marijuana, hard drugs, and weapons in contraband data.

agenda_items.title: Underground Private Utility Installation and Cost Recovery
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works presented a cost-recovery analysis showing an estimated $3.4 million over two years ($1 million in personnel and $2.4 million in locating and support services) driven by Google Fiber and AT&T deployments alongside general development. Staff noted utilities had been briefed without endorsing any fee hike, and Council discussed the impact on existing utilities such as PSNC while expressing preference for 100 percent fee recovery from utility companies rather than general fund tax subsidies.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Appointments & Setting the Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced unanimous 7-vote appointments for the Human Relations Commission (Franklin Hayes), Housing Authority (Robert Glenn), Recreation Advisory Commission (Kevin Lloyd and Jason Parker), and Durham Planning Commission, as well as a 4-vote appointment for the Passenger Vehicle for Hire Commission. Council then voted unanimously to set the regular meeting agenda with Consent Items 1-31 and Public Hearings 36-41 and 43.

votes.notes: Voice vote passed unanimously at start of session; Eugene Brown and Eddie Davis were noted as on their way during initial roll call and Steve Schewel's roll call response was unclear in ASR audio.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager requested referring Item 42 back to administration for resubmission by City-County Planning in the next cycle.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 24, 2015
meetings.executive_summary: At its June 24, 2015 special meeting, the Durham City Council confirmed four appointees to the Civilian Police Review Board by ballot and unanimously approved (7-0) a $500,000 funding request for the Durham Housing Authority and Development Ventures Incorporated to support public housing redevelopment. Council then passed a maximum $6 million, 15-year economic development incentive agreement with Wexford Science & Technology to redevelop the Chesterfield Building (exact numeric tally not stated in the transcript excerpt), overcoming criticism of the county's $2.6 million share and fiscal return questions. On Item 4, council passed a preliminary economic development incentive agreement of up to $5.25 million over 15 years with Longfellow Real Estate Partners for the Durham Innovation District by a 6-1 split vote—Ayes: Bill Bell, Cora Cole-McFadden, Eugene Brown, Steve Schewel, Eddie Davis, and Don Moffitt; Nay: Diane Catotti—after debate over tax-revenue percentages, deferred occupancy thresholds, and public park access, followed by Catotti's announcement that she would not seek reelection.

agenda_items.title: Council Memorials and Affordable Housing Milestones
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Eddie Davis noted the recent passing of Lewis Cheek and former advisory committee member and council candidate Edward Quon. Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden reported attending the groundbreaking for Phase Two of Denson Apartments for veterans and a homeownership celebration at Southside, praising the city's visible affordable housing progress.

agenda_items.title: Confirmation of Civilian Police Review Board Members
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council cast paper ballots to confirm nominees to the Civilian Police Review Board as recommended by the City Manager. At the conclusion of the meeting, Mayor Bill Bell announced that council confirmed all four appointees.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (all four appointees confirmed by ballot)

agenda_items.title: Durham Housing Authority and Development Ventures Inc. $500,000 Funding Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Durham Housing Authority CEO Dallas Parks presented a $500,000 funding request to support completion, lease-up, operating, and tax-credit guarantees for DHA/DVI affordable housing redevelopments, including Morreene Road and units for formerly homeless residents. Council Member Steve Schewel strongly endorsed DHA's emergence as a developer, and Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden's motion to approve—with Council Member Diane Catotti requesting a 250-to-300 minimum unit target in the contract—passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Wexford Science & Technology (Chesterfield Building)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Office of Economic and Workforce Development Director Kevin Dick presented a proposed $6 million city incentive over 15 years (alongside a $2.6 million county commitment over five years, historic and new markets tax credits, and private equity) for Wexford Science & Technology to adaptively reuse the former Chesterfield factory into lab and office space, conditioned on workforce, M/WBE, and nights/weekends parking commitments. Some council members criticized the county's contribution as 'puny and measly' and questioned the fiscal return, while Mayor Bell defended the county's constraints and warned the building would continue deteriorating without the deal before council voted to approve.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Preliminary Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Longfellow Real Estate Partners (Durham Innovation District)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Kevin Dick presented a preliminary incentive agreement not to exceed $5.25 million over 15 years (net present value roughly $3 million) with Longfellow Real Estate Partners to build Class A lab and office space in the Durham Innovation District, with Michelle Jameson speaking in support. Diane Catotti opposed the 70% tax-revenue share, the deferral of the 70% occupancy requirement until year three, and insufficient public parking and county participation, while Don Moffitt and Steve Schewel questioned whether the planned park would be truly public and worried about future phases seeking subsidies; the agreement passed 6-1 with Catotti voting no.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Diane Catotti Retirement Announcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the vote on Item 4, Council Member Diane Catotti announced that after 12 years on the City Council she had decided not to file for reelection the following month. She thanked her colleagues, staff, husband, and family while pledging to continue working hard through her remaining five months in office.

votes.item_title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Wexford Science & Technology (Chesterfield Building)
votes.notes: Exact numeric vote tally was not spoken in the transcript excerpt ('It passes'), though Steve Schewel later referenced disagreeing with the Mayor on both this item and Item 4.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff recommended negotiating a $6 million, 15-year incentive for Wexford Science & Technology's adaptive reuse of the former Chesterfield factory alongside $2.6 million from Durham County. After debate over parking requirements, tax returns, and whether the county was contributing enough, Mayor Bell defended the deal as essential to prevent further deterioration of the historic building, and the motion passed.

votes.item_title: Preliminary Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Longfellow Real Estate Partners, LLC (Durham Innovation District)
votes.notes: Diane Catotti was explicitly identified on the record as the sole dissenting vote ('It passes six to one with Council Member Catotti voting no').
votes.discussion_detail: Staff presented an up-to-$5.25 million, 15-year incentive for Longfellow Real Estate Partners to construct speculative Class A lab and office space in the Durham Innovation District. Diane Catotti questioned deferring the 70% occupancy requirement until year three, objected to the 70% future tax-revenue share and low county contribution, and voted no; Don Moffitt questioned whether the proposed park would be genuinely public and Steve Schewel voiced concern about future phases seeking subsidies, though both joined the 6-1 majority.

disagreements.issue: Wexford Science & Technology (Chesterfield Building) $6M Incentive and County Contribution Share
disagreements.summary: Council members debated the fiscal return of the city's $6 million, 15-year incentive for Wexford Science & Technology's adaptive reuse of the Chesterfield Building and whether Durham County's $2.6 million contribution was adequate.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support the city incentive as a necessary partnership with the county to rescue and activate the deteriorating Chesterfield Building.
side_a_arguments: Adaptive reuse of the former factory into lab space is cost-prohibitive after multiple failed redevelopment attempts.
Durham County carries a much larger budget and school funding mandates and is not obligated to contribute, yet its $2.6 million makes the deal viable.
Without the agreement, the Chesterfield Building will remain an eyesore and continue to deteriorate, whereas completion generates long-term net revenues.
disagreements.side_b_position: Question the city's fiscal exposure and criticize Durham County's $2.6 million commitment as disproportionately small.
side_b_arguments: The county's $2.6 million contribution over five years is inadequate relative to the city's $6 million over 15 years and the parking deck arrangements.
The fiscal and tax return structure requires stricter scrutiny before committing millions in city incentives.
disagreements.resolution: Motion passed (exact numeric tally not stated in the transcript excerpt).

disagreements.issue: Longfellow Real Estate Partners (Durham Innovation District) $5.25M Preliminary Incentive Terms
disagreements.summary: Council debated the subsidy level, year-three occupancy threshold, public park language, public parking availability, and future-phase subsidy expectations for the Durham Innovation District incentive.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the preliminary incentive agreement to catalyze Class A lab and office development on underutilized downtown parcels.
side_a_arguments: The project creates needed Class A office and high-tech lab space, attracts high-wage jobs, and increases long-term property tax revenue.
Deferring the 70% occupancy threshold until the third payment year reflects the leasing timeline for speculative lab buildings.
Staff addressed closed-session concerns regarding the proposed public park and future-phase expectations.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the incentive terms as overly generous to the developer with insufficient public return and county participation.
side_b_arguments: Rebating 70% of future tax revenues over 15 years is too high.
Deferring the 70% occupancy requirement until year three is overly generous given claimed market demand.
A higher percentage of parking should be open to the public and Durham County should contribute more.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 6-1 (Diane Catotti voting No; Don Moffitt and Steve Schewel voted Aye while flagging park-access and future-phase incentive concerns).

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Opened by Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden before Mayor Bill Bell arrived to preside, the City Council worked through a 65-item agenda featuring Council Member Eugene Brown's announcement that he would not seek re-election, budget and strategic plan items, and infrastructure financing for unfinished subdivisions. Early in the session, the six members present voted 6-0 to approve the City Manager's priority items, suspend the rules, and adopt a consistency statement for the denial of Item 65 (108 Celeste Parking Lot rezoning). On Item 53 (Stonehill Estates and Ravenstone subdivisions street and stormwater completion), Council unanimously suspended the rules (7-0) and then passed a motion by a 6-1 show-of-hands vote approving a $1,134,000 City contribution option and directing staff to schedule a public hearing; the transcript digest did not identify the individual member who cast the lone Nay vote by name among the seven seated members (Bill Bell, Cora Cole-McFadden, Eugene Brown, Diane Catotti, Steve Schewel, Eddie Davis, and Don Moffitt). Council also deferred Item 63 (Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard / Business 15-501 road configuration) to June 15 to address business owners' traffic and queuing concerns, scheduled a June 8 continuation session for remaining items, and voted unanimously to enter closed session on an economic incentive agreement.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items & Item 65 (108 Celeste Parking Lot Consistency Statement)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield apologized for the 65-item agenda, scheduled Item 15 (Police Headquarters Complex layout) for a 2:30 PM time-certain, moved Item 64 (FY15-16 employee health benefits) to next week, and requested immediate action on Item 65 to adopt a required consistency statement for Monday's denial of the 108 Celeste parking lot rezoning. Council approved the priority items, suspended the rules, and adopted Item 65 unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Eugene Brown Retirement Announcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Eugene Brown, serving since 2003, announced that he would not be a candidate for re-election. Mayor Bell and colleagues thanked Brown for his long service and continued contributions through the remainder of his term.

agenda_items.title: Consent & Planning Agenda Review (Strategic Plan, Budget/CIP, TIGER Grant)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed appointments and departmental items, praising staff for the FY 2016-2018 City of Durham Strategic Plan update (Item 13) and the FY16 Planning Department Work Program (Item 16) amid rapid growth. Items discussed or pulled included the FY 2015-2016 budget and FY 2016-2021 CIP (Item 15), parking fees and management (Items 17-18), and the Belt Line Trail Master Plan TIGER grant (Item 20).

agenda_items.title: Completion of Street and Stormwater Infrastructure in Stonehill Estates and Ravenstone Subdivisions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney explained that a federal judge had ruled against the City's interpretation of developer performance and stormwater bonds, though staff maintained the bonds were validly drafted and tightened future bond language. After residents urged greater municipal credit and relief from assessment liens, Council suspended the rules and approved by a 6-1 show-of-hands vote a $1,134,000 City contribution option and a public hearing in August or September.

agenda_items.title: Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard (Business 15-501) Road Configuration & Continuation Scheduling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members reported meeting with Boulevard business owners who supported safety improvements but feared traffic volume impacts, queue backups, and business losses from a proposed road diet. Council agreed to move Item 63 to June 15 for additional traffic data and scheduled a Monday continuation work session for Items 29, 43, 49, 50, and 64 before voting to enter closed session on an economic incentive agreement.

votes.item_title: Approval of City Manager's Priority Items
votes.notes: Voice vote taken while Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden presided prior to Mayor Bill Bell's arrival.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved Manager's agenda adjustments including time-certain for Item 15 and moving Item 64 to the supplemental work session.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules to Vote on Item 65 (108 Celeste Parking Lot Consistency Statement)
votes.notes: Voice vote prior to Mayor Bell's arrival.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended rules so planning staff would not have to remain for public hearings.

votes.item_title: Item 65: Adopt Consistency Statement for Denial of 108 Celeste Parking Lot Zoning Map Change
votes.notes: Voice vote prior to Mayor Bell's arrival at 00:08:40.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted the required statutory consistency statement for Council's prior denial of the rezoning.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules to Vote on Item 53 (Stonehill Estates and Ravenstone Infrastructure)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously by voice vote with all seven members seated.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended rules to act on the Stonehill Estates and Ravenstone cost-split proposal during the work session.

votes.item_title: Item 53: Stonehill Estates & Ravenstone Infrastructure Completion ($1,134,000 City Contribution & Public Hearing)
votes.notes: Vote was taken by show of hands and announced as 6-1; individual member names for the six Ayes and the lone Nay were not read aloud into the audio transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the page-7 option setting the City's contribution at $1,134,000 (just over 50 percent of the cost) and directing staff to schedule an August/September public hearing.

votes.item_title: Enter Closed Session (Economic Incentive Agreement)
votes.notes: Passed by voice vote without opposition.
votes.discussion_detail: Entered closed session to discuss an economic incentive agreement.

disagreements.issue: Stonehill Estates and Ravenstone Infrastructure Cost Split ($1,134,000 City Contribution)
disagreements.summary: Following an adverse federal court ruling on subdivision performance bonds, Council split 6-1 over approving an option placing $1,134,000 (slightly over 50 percent) of street and stormwater completion costs on the City while assessing remaining costs against homeowners.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the $1,134,000 City contribution option and move forward to a formal public hearing.
side_a_arguments: City Attorney defended the original bonds as standard when issued despite the judge's ruling and tightened future bond language.
The $1,134,000 option covered slightly more than half the completion burden while advancing a resolution before the public hearing.
disagreements.side_b_position: Opposed the $1,134,000 cost-split motion (lone dissenter; residents sought full credit for tax/roadway funds already paid).
side_b_arguments: Public speakers contended the City held sufficient face-value bond coverage and homeowners should receive full credit rather than assessment liens.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 6-1 by show of hands (individual Aye and Nay voters not named in the audio transcript); staff directed to schedule a public hearing in August or September.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 1, 2015
meetings.executive_summary: The June 1, 2015 Durham City Council meeting began with a recognition of Carrington Middle School musicians and a unanimous 7-0 vote accepting the City Clerk's priority item ruling a protest petition on Item 30 insufficient. Council then opened the public hearing on the proposed FY 2015-16 budget through its third annual E-Town Hall moderated by Ken Smith, addressing property tax rates and affordable housing, a nearly $3 million revenue loss from state repeal of business privilege license fees, youth employment, police body cameras, and $2.1 million in arts funding. Following a middle transcript gap, council engaged in a sharp late-night debate over an NCDOT resurfacing and lane-reconfiguration ('road diet') plan for Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard opposed by corridor business owners; after an initial 5-2 vote on Don Moffitt's motion to approve staff's 3-lane restriping plan was reopened for clarification, council passed Eugene Brown's substitute-to-the-substitute motion 4-3—Ayes: Bill Bell, Cora Cole-McFadden, Eugene Brown, and Eddie Davis; Nays: Diane Catotti, Don Moffitt, and Steve Schewel—to proceed with state-funded resurfacing while deferring the striping decision until later in June.

agenda_items.title: Recognition of Carrington Middle School Musical Performance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell thanked Carrington Middle School students and their music director for performing in the City Hall lobby prior to the meeting. He praised their engagement and invited them to return in the future.

agenda_items.title: City Clerk Priority Item: Item 30 Zoning Map Change Protest Petition Ruled Insufficient
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following no priority items from the City Manager or City Attorney, the City Clerk reported that a protest petition filed on Item 30 (zoning map change) had been ruled insufficient. Council moved, seconded, and accepted the priority item 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Proposed FY 2015-16 Budget Public Hearing and Third Annual E-Town Hall Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell opened the FY 2015-16 budget public hearing with a 45-minute E-Town Hall moderated by WRAL anchor Ken Smith featuring questions submitted online and on audience cards. Council members discussed keeping tax rates sufficient to fund affordable housing (Mayor Bell), replacing nearly $3 million lost from state elimination of business privilege license fees (Eugene Brown), year-round youth activities and private-sector jobs (Cora Cole-McFadden), funding police body cameras for all officers alongside federal grant applications (Eddie Davis), and $2.1 million in arts and cultural support (Don Moffitt).

agenda_items.title: Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard NCDOT Resurfacing and Lane Reconfiguration (5 Lanes vs. 3 Lanes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff explained that NCDOT's summer resurfacing contract prompted review of a restriping plan converting Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard to three lanes with bike lanes and 21 parking spaces, while corridor business owners testified against lane reductions and requested speed enforcement and a Hope Valley Road signal instead. Council split over whether to adopt staff's 3-lane reconfiguration immediately or delay, briefly voting 5-2 on Don Moffitt's motion to adopt staff's plan before reopening for clarification; council then passed Eugene Brown's substitute-to-the-substitute motion 4-3 to accept NCDOT resurfacing now and decide striping later in June.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-3 (Ayes: Bell, Cole-McFadden, Brown, Davis; Nays: Catotti, Moffitt, Schewel)

votes.item_title: Acceptance of City Clerk Priority Item (Item 30 Protest Petition Ruled Insufficient)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named on the record.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Clerk announced that a protest petition filed on Item 30 (zoning map change) had been ruled insufficient. Council moved, seconded, and unanimously accepted the priority item 7-0.

votes.item_title: Substitute-to-the-Substitute Motion: Proceed with NCDOT Resurfacing of Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard and Defer Striping Decision
votes.notes: Earlier reopened 5-2 vote on Don Moffitt's substitute motion (with Mayor Bell voting no) was vacated/superseded upon reopening and adoption of Eugene Brown's substitute-to-the-substitute.
votes.discussion_detail: Following business-owner opposition to reducing Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard from five lanes to three lanes, council first moved to delay for one two-week cycle, then voted 5-2 on a substitute motion by Don Moffitt to approve staff's 3-lane restriping plan before reopening that vote for procedural clarification. Council Member Eugene Brown then moved a substitute-to-the-substitute to accept NCDOT-funded resurfacing immediately and return by late June to decide the striping configuration; staff noted NCDOT would revert to existing 5-lane striping if council did not decide within six weeks, and the motion passed 4-3 with Diane Catotti, Don Moffitt, and Steve Schewel voting no.

disagreements.issue: Durham-Chapel Hill Boulevard Lane Reconfiguration (3-Lane Road Diet vs. 5-Lane Status Quo / Delay)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 over whether to adopt staff's proposed three-lane bike/parking reconfiguration immediately or accept NCDOT resurfacing while deferring the striping decision due to business-owner opposition.
disagreements.side_a_position: Proceed with NCDOT-funded resurfacing immediately and defer the striping decision until late June to allow further discussion with affected businesses.
side_a_arguments: Durham should not turn down state NCDOT resurfacing funding for a deteriorated corridor.
A large share of local business owners along the short corridor opposed the lane reduction and felt insufficiently consulted, signaling a communication breakdown.
The proposed plan adds only 21 parking spaces, and council still has until the end of June to finalize striping.
disagreements.side_b_position: Decide the striping configuration directly rather than adopting a convoluted deferral, with supporters of the 3-lane plan arguing delay jeopardizes safety and parking improvements.
side_b_arguments: Slowing traffic and adding bike lanes and parking makes pulling out of corridor restaurants and shops safer and will attract more customers.
Deferring to an unspecified later vote is procedurally convoluted and risks missing NCDOT's summer contract deadline or overloading the next 63-item agenda.
Council should vote directly up-or-down on the three-lane vs. five-lane striping rather than deferring.
disagreements.resolution: Eugene Brown's substitute-to-the-substitute motion to proceed with NCDOT resurfacing and revisit striping later passed 4-3 (Ayes: Bell, Cole-McFadden, Brown, Davis; Nays: Catotti, Moffitt, Schewel).

meetings.title: City Council Budget Work Session FY 2015-2016
meetings.executive_summary: Opened by Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden before Mayor Bill Bell arrived, the City Council held day two of its FY 2015-2016 budget work sessions focusing on Goal 2 (Safe and Secure Community) and City-County Planning. Public safety leaders presented Emergency Communications (911) reorganization and dispatch standards, Fire Department response and inspection metrics, and Police Department initiatives including expanded crime scene investigation capacity and online low-level crime reporting. Council members questioned Fire Chief Dan Curia on why city fire stations were bearing multi-million-dollar costs to provide medical first response amid Durham County EMS response delays, and discussed low employee engagement scores among shift firefighters. Later, City-County Planning presented its $3.79 million budget (50/50 City-County funded, 44 of 46 FTEs funded), highlighting 25 percent staff turnover, over 2,800 residential plan reviews, and code-review bottlenecks from new state wall-bracing rules. No formal votes were taken during this budget review session.

agenda_items.title: Goal 2 Overview & Emergency Communications (911) FY16 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Fire Chief Dan Curia and Police Deputy Chief Larry Smith outlined Goal 2 initiatives, including adding CSI capacity, launching 'Police to Community' online reporting for minor thefts, and building 3-to-5-year departmental staffing plans. Emergency Communications Director Jim Soukup reviewed 911 organizational shifts, NFPA dispatch time benchmarks designed to avoid sending unnecessary apparatus, and EMD text initiatives.

agenda_items.title: Fire Department FY16 Budget, EMS First Response & Inspection Metrics
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Curia reported response time variations across city districts and noted that only 40 percent of the department's eight fire inspectors met goals this year (down from 75 percent last year after 8,000 inspections). Council questioned spending millions on city fire stations to cover first-response medical calls due to Durham County EMS delays, with Curia explaining firefighters respond only to life-threatening emergencies while the County is nearly doubling street medics, and also discussed 50 percent engagement among shift firefighters.

agenda_items.title: City-County Planning Department FY16 Budget & Workload Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning presented a $3,788,261 budget (93 percent personnel, 50/50 City-County split, 44 funded of 46 authorized FTEs) fully offset by program revenues, alongside implementation of digital plan review. Staff reported 25 percent turnover, over 2,800 projected residential plan reviews, delays caused by new state residential wall-bracing code requirements, and mixed experiences with Joint City-County Planning Committee alignment on ordinances like wireless facilities.

agenda_items.title: Budget Schedule & Follow-Up Topics
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council and the City Manager reviewed the upcoming Monday budget town hall public hearing and tentative follow-up meeting schedule. agenda_items.title: General Fund Revenues, Tax Rate & Solid Waste Fund Allocation

agenda_items.title: Public Works Utility Locate Surge (Google Fiber/AT&T), Sidewalks & Stormwater

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Opened briefly by Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden before Mayor Bill Bell assumed the chair, the Durham City Council reviewed consent items, poverty reduction and Complete Streets updates, and competing FY 2015-2016 employee health insurance proposals. Council approved the City Manager's priority items by unanimous voice vote—referring back two condemnation items (Items 14 and 15, including 339 University Drive) for insufficient federal notice time and removing Item 22. Following a Complete Streets presentation noting African Americans comprised 60 percent of pedestrian crash victims in Durham versus 40 percent of the population, Council members requested a draft Complete Streets resolution coordinated with Durham County. On Item 16 (employee health benefits), HR staff presented an Aetna recommendation citing $2.2 million in annual discount-penalty guarantees, while Blue Cross Blue Shield urged a 10-month bridge with $500,000 at risk until its accountable care network launches in July 2016; Council placed Item 16 on the General Business Agenda for a side-by-side drug formulary and cost comparison. Council unanimously approved setting the regular agenda and entering closed session.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items (Refer Back Items 14 & 15; Remove Item 22)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager recommended referring back Items 14 and 15 (proposed property condemnations, including 339 University Drive for a sidewalk project) because federal notice timelines were not met, and removing Item 22 as redundant. Council approved the priority items unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Consent & Public Hearing Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed consent items including the April 2015 Health Benefits Performance Audit (Item 5), financial audit (Item 6), a 0.88-acre greenway trail acquisition praised by Council (Item 13), and a public art agreement (Item 18). Public hearings covered the proposed FY 2015-2016 budget and CIP (Item 25), Barr Creek Assembly (Items 26-27), 108 Celeste parking lot (Item 28), Parker Plaza (Item 29), North-Mindum residential (Item 30), Circle K Duke Street (Item 31), Hobson Road annexation (Item 32), and Ridgeway/Ridgerate street closing (Item 33).

agenda_items.title: Poverty Reduction Initiative Update & Complete Streets Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff briefed Council on Poverty Reduction Initiative efforts including senior weatherization, a boarded structures action plan, and resident fair-housing outreach. Transportation staff then presented Complete Streets principles, highlighting that 60 percent of Durham pedestrian crash victims are African American, and Council members requested a draft Complete Streets resolution aligned with Durham County and voiced support for road diets.

agenda_items.title: FY 2015-2016 Employee Health Benefits Recommendation (Aetna vs. Blue Cross Blue Shield)

BCBS representatives pitched a 10-month bridge placing $500,000 at risk ahead of their July 2016 accountable care offering with Duke Health; Council directed staff to evaluate both proposals using the same 7,000-drug formulary formula and place Item 16 on the General Business Agenda.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting
meetings.executive_summary: Presided over by Mayor Bill Bell, the Durham City Council held a special meeting focused on the Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit project and U.S. Department of Justice technical assistance for the Durham Police Department. GoTriangle representatives presented detailed engineering constraints east of Alston Avenue—citing North Carolina Railroad plans for a four-track corridor and single-track delay risks—explaining why the Alston station must shift roughly a quarter-mile west toward Murphy Street ahead of the February 2016 federal environmental deadline. On the rail yard maintenance facility, Council reviewed Planning staff findings that three of five candidate sites were incompatible with surrounding residential areas, leaving Cornwallis Road or an Alston site costing $20-$30 million more, while deferring an official vote until Chapel Hill weighs in. On policing, Council reviewed four tracks of DOJ technical assistance, community policing/PAC funding structure, juvenile age laws, gun-crime enforcement with ATF, and the completion of Fair and Impartial Policing training by nearly 500 officers, voting unanimously by voice vote to accept the DOJ technical assistance offer.

agenda_items.title: Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit: Alston Avenue Station & Rail Yard Site Analysis
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GoTriangle staff (Patrick McDonough, Dave Charters, and Catherine Eggleston) compared Durham-Chapel Hill transit ridership to Salt Lake City and Charlotte and detailed North Carolina Railroad corridor constraints east of Alston Avenue that prevent dual-track station operation and jeopardize the February 2016 FEIS deadline. Staff recommended shifting the station about a quarter-mile west near Murphy Street, and Council discussed Planning's assessment narrowing feasible rail yard sites to Cornwallis Road or Alston ($20-$30 million higher) ahead of Chapel Hill's input.

agenda_items.title: U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) Technical Assistance & Police Community Relations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council and Police leadership reviewed four tracks of proposed DOJ technical assistance covering communications, tactical violent crime peer networks, and police-community relations, alongside discussion of PAC meetings ($1,200 per PAC shifted to NIS), treating 16- and 17-year-olds as adults, ATF gun tracing, and nearly 500 officers completing Fair and Impartial Policing training. Council voted unanimously by voice vote to accept the DOJ technical assistance offer.

votes.notes: Voice vote passed unanimously; initial roll call captured Catotti, Moffitt, and Schewel with Cole-McFadden on her way and Mayor Bell presiding.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted the DOJ's offer of four tracks of technical assistance for the Durham Police Department.

meetings.title: Proposed FY '15 - '16 Budget Presentation
meetings.executive_summary: This May 20, 2015 video is a standalone presentation recording of City Manager Tom Bonfield delivering General Business Item 19, the Proposed FY 2015-16 Budget and FY 2016-2021 Capital Improvement Plan, to the Durham City Council and public. Bonfield presented a $386.5 million total budget (down nearly 1%) and a $170.2 million General Fund budget (down nearly 3%) with no property tax rate increase (59.12 cents per $100 assessed value), offsetting over $2.9 million lost from the state's repeal of the business privilege license tax and establishing a dedicated tax allocation for solid waste while maintaining a projected 21% fund balance. Key spending priorities included $91.4 million for public safety with all sworn positions funded, $2 million for street paving, $500,000 for sidewalks, a continued half-cent tax for parks maintenance, a 3% water and sewer rate increase, an Open Government Portal, and public input through the June 1 E-Town Hall; no formal votes occurred on the budget presentation itself.

agenda_items.title: Proposed FY 2015-16 Budget and FY 2016-2021 Capital Improvement Plan Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the tail end of a prior 7-0 consent vote, Mayor Bill Bell introduced General Business Item 19 for City Manager Tom Bonfield's formal budget presentation. Bonfield outlined a $386.5 million total budget and $170.2 million General Fund budget holding the tax rate flat at 59.12 cents, replacing over $2.9 million in repealed business privilege license revenue, creating a dedicated solid waste tax allocation, and using $1.7 million of fund balance while maintaining roughly 21% reserves.

agenda_items.title: Customer Service, Arts, Open Government Portal, and Neighborhood Initiatives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Bonfield proposed a citywide customer service review, an additional Durham One Call representative, and a resident problem-reporting smartphone app. He also highlighted continued support for cultural festivals such as Full Frame, the American Dance Festival, and Art of Cool, a planned Durham Sports Commission partnership with the county and CVB, a new Open Government Portal launching the next month, and a mobile-friendly city website redesign.

agenda_items.title: Public Safety Funding Allocation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Bonfield reported that public safety accounts for $91.4 million of the proposed budget, with nearly 62% directed to law enforcement. While no new police officer or firefighter positions were added for FY 2015-16, all existing sworn positions remained fully funded alongside ongoing deployment reviews to plan for future personnel needs as Durham grows.

agenda_items.title: Infrastructure, Street Paving, Parks Maintenance, Utilities, and Capital Projects
agenda_items.discussion_summary: To address physical asset backlogs and resident survey priorities, the proposed budget increased deferred maintenance funding to $600,000, added $108,000 for asset management software, boosted street paving to $2 million alongside $500,000 for sidewalks, and continued the dedicated half-cent tax (~$1.2 million) for parks maintenance. It also proposed an average 3% water and sewer rate increase generating $2.9 million for line maintenance, no stormwater rate increase, and more than $12.9 million in capital projects.

agenda_items.title: Public Input Schedule and Mayor Bell's Closing Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Bonfield invited residents to submit budget feedback via email, social media, YouTube, and Durham One Call ahead of the June 1 E-Town Hall and thanked Budget and Management Services Director Bertha Johnson and department directors. Mayor Bill Bell commended the balanced, no-tax-increase proposal as a strong foundation for upcoming council budget deliberations.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 18, 2015
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 18, 2015 regular meeting, the Durham City Council issued a National Public Works Week proclamation to Director Marvin Williams and unanimously approved the consent agenda 7-0 (moving Items 19, 24, and 29 to the General Business Agenda). Under General Business, City Manager Tom Bonfield presented the Proposed FY 2015-16 Budget ($386.5 million total, $170.2 million General Fund, unchanged 59.12-cent property tax rate) and FY 2016-2021 Capital Improvement Plan ahead of late-May department reviews and the June 1 E-Town Hall. Council then voted 7-0 to approve an interlocal agreement with Durham County establishing the Durham Workforce Development Board under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act of 2014, and voted 7-0 following a public hearing to grant The Jenson Group, LLC a second extension through July 31, 2015 to complete The Durham Hotel redevelopment.

agenda_items.title: National Public Works Week Proclamation

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden excused absent and Mayor Bill Bell arriving shortly after roll call to preside, the City Council reviewed utility rates, light rail alignment, workforce development, and citizen accessibility concerns. Early in the session, the four members present unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items (including supplemental Item 29 for the Durham Workforce Development Board interlocal agreement) and the City Attorney's request for a closed session on *Ledbetter v. City of Durham*. During Citizens Matters, former Council Member Angela Langley urged stronger ADA enforcement after encountering inaccessible non-automated doors at a new West Chapel Hill Street residence and damaged sidewalks, while another speaker advocated increased FY15-16 funding for senior services. On the Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit project (Item 23), Council discussed why single-track constraints ruled out an east-of-Alston station and heard that three of five candidate rail yard sites were incompatible with residential land uses, leaving Cornwallis or Alston as primary options. Council also questioned baseline house-size assumptions on water/sewer capital facility fees (Item 11) and unanimously set the regular meeting agenda by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: City Manager & City Attorney Priority Items (WIOA Interlocal & Closed Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager flagged presentations for Items 9 (Southeast Regional Lift Station service area fee) and 10 (FY15-16 water and sewer rates), noted Item 25 citizen Otis Lyons would not appear, and added supplemental Item 29 (Durham Workforce Development Board interlocal agreement under WIOA 2014). Council unanimously approved both the Manager's priority items and the City Attorney's request for a closed session regarding Ledbetter v. City of Durham and one unnamed claim.

agenda_items.title: Consent & Public Hearing Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed departmental items including Southeast Regional Lift Station fees (Item 9), FY15-16 water and sewer rates and capital facility fees (Items 10-11), Wake County tax collection consolidation (Item 12), CM Herndon Park artificial turf soccer field (Item 13), compensation and classification recommendations (Item 14), sidewalk repair/inspection contracts (Items 17-18), FY15-16 budget/CIP scheduling (Item 19), urban forest recommendations (Item 21), Ome Street condition report (Item 22), and the Gentian Group downtown incentive amendment (Item 24).

agenda_items.title: Citizens Matters: Youth Programming, ADA Accessibility & Senior Funding
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Lawrence discussed youth/teen engagement resources, and former Council Member Angela Langley raised ADA accessibility barriers at 605 West Chapel Hill Street and broken sidewalks forcing wheelchair users into busy streets. Beverly Stevenson urged Council to account for a projected 44 percent growth in Durham's senior population over the next decade in the FY15-16 budget.

agenda_items.title: Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit Project: Alston Station & Rail Yard Sites
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff explained why single-track operations east of Alston Avenue would cause system-wide cascading delays and reviewed shifting the station west of Alston near Pettigrew/Murphy. Council members noted that Planning's joint assessment effectively eliminated three of five candidate rail yard sites as incompatible with residential neighborhoods, leaving Cornwallis (requiring rezoning only) or Alston ($20-$30 million costlier).

agenda_items.title: Water & Sewer Capital Facility Fee Comparison & Setting the Regular Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members questioned Utility Finance Manager Martha Ziegler on why the municipal comparison chart used a 2,401-square-foot home size to compare flat-meter and square-footage-based fees. Council then unanimously set the regular meeting agenda: Consent Items 1-18, GBA Items 19 and 29, GBA Public Hearing Item 24, with Items 20-23 and 25-28 disposed.

votes.item_title: Approval of City Manager's Priority Items
votes.notes: Voice vote prior to Mayor Bill Bell's arrival; Cora Cole-McFadden had an excused absence and Eugene Brown was not recorded at roll call.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved priority scheduling for Items 9, 10, 25, and supplemental Item 29 (WIOA interlocal).

votes.item_title: Approval of City Attorney's Priority Items (Closed Session: Ledbetter v. City of Durham)
votes.notes: Voice vote prior to Mayor Bill Bell's arrival.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved closed session request under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) for Ledbetter v. City of Durham and one unnamed claim.

votes.item_title: Setting the Regular Meeting Agenda (Consent 1-18; GBA 19, 29; Public Hearing 24)
votes.notes: Voice vote carried without opposition with Mayor Bell presiding and Cora Cole-McFadden excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Set Consent Items 1-18, GBA Items 19 and 29, and GBA Public Hearing Item 24, disposing of Items 20-23 and 25-28.
