meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting May 19, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members convened on May 19, 2014, opening with recognitions for National Public Works Week and a briefing from Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson on emergency recovery from a confirmed EF1 tornado the prior weekend. Council unanimously approved the consent agenda (excluding Item 2), heard City Manager Tom Bonfield's formal presentation of the proposed $386.7 million FY 2014-2015 budget, and approved a 7.5% stormwater rate increase, the 123.5-acre Corners at Brier Creek consolidated annexation and initial zoning, and a Rougemont watershed text amendment. Council also referred a tree-coverage UDO text amendment back to staff and approved a Google Fiber network hut license agreement 7-0 after public comment urging local hiring.

agenda_items.title: Recognitions, National Public Works Week Proclamation, and Tornado Recovery Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell recognized Cubmaster Emeritus Masony Brooks for 43 years with Pack 137 at St. Joseph AME Church and proclaimed National Public Works Week for Director Marvin Williams and department staff. At Councilmember Don Moffitt's request, Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson briefed Council on the multi-agency response to an EF1 tornado and torrential rain the prior Thursday night, noting debris clearing by Public Works, General Services, Solid Waste, Parks and Recreation, the Sheriff's Office, Red Cross, and Baptist Men's Association. Councilmember Eddie Davis and Moffitt also praised Parks and Recreation staff for hosting the Bimbe Festival at Rock Quarry Park.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Minutes, Southside HOME Funds, Compensation Plan, Water/Sewer Rates & Capital Projects)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the consent agenda with the exception of Item 2 (Network Hut License Agreement with Google), which was pulled by resident Victoria Peterson. Approved items included council minutes, a $500,000 HOME Investment Partnerships amendment with Southside Revitalization Phase 1 LP, renewal of the Urban Search and Rescue MOA, compensation and classification plan recommendations, FY 2014-2015 water and sewer rates (averaging 3% increase), water and sewer capital facilities fee updates, water/sewer master plan engineering contract amendment #2, and the Turnage Heights lift station abandonment project.

agenda_items.title: Proposed FY 2014-2015 Budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented the proposed $386.7 million total budget ($173.6 million general fund) for FY 2014-2015, proposing a 1.29-cent property tax increase to 58.04 cents per $100 assessed value to fund voter-approved debt service and 31 police and fire positions previously supported by expired grants. The budget restored differentiated pay-for-performance raises (3% general, 3.5% police/fire), increased street repaving to $1 million, budgeted $400,000 for sidewalks, and outlined a potential half-cent tax option for parks maintenance at upcoming workshops starting May 28. During public comment, Victoria Peterson praised fiber initiatives but urged addressing violent crime, arrests, and indigent defense delays in the Durham County Jail.

agenda_items.title: Unified Development Ordinance Text Amendment – Tree Coverage Calculations (TC13-00002)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young of the Planning Department reported that TC13-00002 regarding tree coverage calculations was first heard February 3 and continued to May 19, and that the applicant had recently requested referral back to the administration to make modifications. Staff recommended closing the public hearing and referring the item back to the administration to be re-advertised at the applicant's cost. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation – The Corners at Brier Creek Initial Zoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented a consolidated utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation petition, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning for approximately 123.5 acres at the northern corner of T.W. Alexander Drive and US Highway 70, permitting up to 141 single-family homes or a place of worship with adequate utility capacity and revenue-positive fiscal impact. Attorney Patrick Byker and engineer Tommy Craven represented the development team, and staff noted a scrivener's error in Attachment 11 correcting the hearing date to May 19. Following the 7-0 vote, Mayor Bell and Byker discussed a 1.07-acre boundary overlap in Raleigh's jurisdiction resulting from the T.W. Alexander extension that might require a local legislative act if not resolved administratively.

agenda_items.title: Unified Development Ordinance Text Amendment – Watershed Protection Overlay, Rural Village (TC13-00003)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented a text amendment to Article 8 of the UDO modifying lot size and impervious surface limits within the Rougemont Rural Village, which lies entirely within Durham County jurisdiction. The amendment was brought to maintain consistency between the county and city versions of the UDO after the Board of County Commissioners adopted it unanimously and the Planning Commission recommended approval 12-0 on February 11, 2014. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Adoption of Proposed Stormwater Rates for FY 2015
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Paul Wiebke of Public Works presented a proposed 7.5% stormwater rate increase effective July 1, 2014, to fund stormwater retrofit capital projects required under Falls Lake Stage 1 existing development rules and NPDES permit compliance. Wiebke noted the 7.5% increase was 1% lower than projected the prior year and would raise annual bills by $2.76 (Tier 1), $5.64 (Tier 2), and $11.28 (Tier 3) for residential customers and roughly $110 for non-residential customers. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Network Hut License Agreement between the City of Durham and Google
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson pulled Consent Item 2, welcoming Google Fiber to Durham while raising concerns that city property sites were not yet specified and urging the city to ensure local hiring—including for more than 200 locally trained copper and fiber workers who often face employment barriers due to criminal records. Mayor Bell responded that while the fiber deployments with Google and AT&T were still in early stages, the city would place strong emphasis on employing local residents if the projects proceed.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, excluding pulled Item 2)
votes.notes: Item 2 (Google Network Hut License Agreement) was pulled by public speaker Victoria Peterson for separate consideration.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell read through the consent agenda headings, covering approval of minutes (Item 1), a $500,000 HOME Investment Partnerships amendment for Southside Revitalization Phase 1 LP (Item 4), renewal of the Urban Search and Rescue MOA (Item 5), compensation and classification plan recommendations (Item 6), FY 2014-2015 water and sewer rates averaging a 3% increase (Item 7), water and sewer capital facilities fee updates (Item 8), a water/sewer master plan engineering contract amendment (Item 9), and the Turnage Heights lift station abandonment project (Item 10). Public speaker Victoria Peterson pulled Item 2 for separate discussion later in the meeting. With no council questions on the remaining items, Council moved, seconded, and approved the consent agenda 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 12: UDO Text Amendment – Tree Coverage Calculations (TC13-00002) Referral Back to Administration
votes.notes: Closed public hearing and referred text amendment back to administration at applicant's request, to be re-advertised at applicant's cost.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Pat Young certified statutory public notice and explained that TC13-00002 regarding tree coverage calculations had first been heard on February 3 and continued to May 19. The applicant subsequently requested that the item be referred back to the administration to make modifications in coordination with staff, with re-notification costs borne by the applicant. Mayor Bell opened the public hearing, noted no council questions and no public speakers, closed the hearing, and entertained a motion to accept the staff recommendation. Council voted 7-0 to refer the text amendment back to the administration.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Consolidated Annexation, Utility Extension Agreement, and Initial Zoning – The Corners at Brier Creek
votes.notes: Approves utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial RR zoning for ~123.5 acres at T.W. Alexander Dr & US 70.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented the consolidated utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation petition, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning for 123.5 acres at T.W. Alexander Drive and US Highway 70, reporting adequate water/sewer capacity and a positive fiscal impact analysis for up to 141 single-family homes or a place of worship, while noting the applicant anticipated seeking higher-density rezoning later. Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and engineer Tommy Craven appeared in support, and staff noted for the record a scrivener's correction changing the order date from the 18th to the 19th. With no public opposition, Councilmember Don Moffitt moved approval and Council passed the item 7-0. After the vote, Mayor Bell and Byker discussed a 1.07-acre sliver lying within Raleigh's jurisdiction due to the T.W. Alexander road extension, noting it could require a local legislative act by the Durham delegation if Raleigh and Durham planners could not resolve it administratively.

votes.item_title: Item 14: UDO Text Amendment – Watershed Protection Overlay, Rural Village (TC13-00003)
votes.notes: Matches county-adopted UDO Article 8 standards for Rougemont Rural Village.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented TC13-00003, amending Article 8 of the Unified Development Ordinance regarding lot size and impervious surface limitations in the Rougemont Rural Village. Because Rougemont lies entirely within Durham County's jurisdiction, there was no direct impact inside city limits, and the amendment was needed solely to keep the city and county versions of the joint UDO consistent after unanimous County approval and a 12-0 Planning Commission recommendation on February 11, 2014. No council members asked questions and no members of the public spoke during the hearing. Council closed the public hearing and approved the text amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 15: Adoption of Proposed Stormwater Rates for FY 2015 (7.5% Increase)
votes.notes: Effective July 1, 2014; funds Falls Lake Stage 1 stormwater retrofits and NPDES compliance.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works representative Paul Wiebke presented the proposed 7.5% stormwater rate increase effective July 1, 2014, explaining that it funds repair, operation, and maintenance of city stormwater systems as well as capital retrofits mandated by Falls Lake watershed rules and the city's NPDES permit. Wiebke noted current rates sit near the middle of benchmark peer cities and that the 7.5% increase was 1% lower than projected the previous year, translating to annual increases of $2.76 for Tier 1, $5.64 for Tier 2, $11.28 for Tier 3 residential customers, and roughly $110 for non-residential accounts. No council questions or public comments were offered during the hearing. Council closed the public hearing and adopted the rate increase 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 2 (Pulled Consent): Network Hut License Agreement between City of Durham and Google
votes.notes: Pulled by Victoria Peterson to raise local hiring and reentry employment concerns.
votes.discussion_detail: Resident Victoria Peterson pulled Item 2 from the consent agenda to ask how many homes Google Fiber would serve, which city properties would host fiber huts, and how the city would ensure Durham residents—particularly low-income residents and over 200 individuals previously trained locally in copper and fiber cabling who face hiring barriers due to felony records—receive installation jobs rather than being bypassed. Mayor Bell replied that the city could not yet answer all project specifics, as both Google and AT&T were still evaluating proposals, but assured Peterson that if fiber projects requiring city support move forward, the city would place strong emphasis on employing local residents. Council then moved, seconded, and approved the Google network hut license agreement 7-0.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 8, 2014 Durham City Council Work Session presided over by Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden, Council unanimously accepted the Acting City Manager's priority items and suspended the rules to approve Item 3, selling city-owned Eastway Village property at 606 Eastway Avenue after staff explained prior second-mortgage outcomes and buyer readiness. Council questioned Community Development staff on Item 4 ($500,000 HOME amendment for Southside Revitalization Phase I LP), receiving assurances that shifting $433,000 from Phase II rental funds and $67,000 from homeownership funds would not delay Phase II's January tax-credit application due to stable federal entitlement projections. Water Management staff presented proposed FY 2015 water and sewer rate updates featuring a 3% typical rate increase, reduced billing call wait times, Watershed Protection Fund spending, and post-2009 irrigation meter rules, while Stormwater staff presented a $13.6 million FY 2015 enterprise budget avoiding a previously projected 8.5% rate hike while funding NPDES and Falls/Jordan Lake Stage 1 capital projects. Council unanimously set the May 19 regular meeting agenda with no split or contested votes.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Acting City Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden called the work session to order at 1:00 p.m., with Cole-McFadden, Eddie Davis, and Steve Schewel answering roll call (Brown and Catotti also called). The Acting City Manager requested rule suspension for Item 3 (606 Eastway Avenue sale) and noted presentations for FY 2015 water/sewer rates, the FY 2015 budget (scheduled for May 19), and FY 2015 stormwater rates, which Council unanimously accepted.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Review and Item 3 (Sale of 606 Eastway Avenue)

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting May 5, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on May 5, 2014, adopting the consent agenda and holding public hearings on the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan for federal HUD and local dedicated housing funds, prior-year HUD grant reconciliations, inspections permit fee updates, the UDI Farm comprehensive plan amendment and RS-20 rezoning (approved 6-0 with Mayor Bell recused due to his employment at UDI CDC), and a street closing adjacent to Lakewood Elementary School. Council also heard extensive testimony from Housing for New Hope clients, Urban Ministries, Durham Community Land Trustees, and the Citizens Advisory Committee during the Annual Action Plan hearing, and reviewed the Durham Police Department's Q1 2014 crime report showing a 36% spike in Part 1 violent crime driven by multi-victim shootings alongside the launch of a juvenile misdemeanor diversion program.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Council Comments, and City Manager Priority Agenda Adjustments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell and Councilmember Steve Schewel presented proclamations for Children's Mental Health Awareness Week, Police Week, Workforce Development Professionals Month, National Drinking Water Week (with student poster contest winners), Older Americans Month, and Fitzgerald Family Day honoring Robert George Fitzgerald and the Pauli Murray Project. Councilmembers Eugene Brown and Cora Cole-McFadden recognized public employees for Public Service Recognition Week, and Mayor Bell promoted an upcoming WNCU radio forum on the Southside neighborhood revitalization. City Manager Tom Bonfield requested holding Consent Item 7 (CASA HOME funds) until after Item 26 and adding Supplemental Item 31 (Q1 Public Safety Report), while Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden flagged a follow-up question on Item 6 regarding how Connecting Youth verifies participants are Durham County residents.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Connecting Youth, Swimming Pool Study, Fire Station 9, Transit-Oriented Housing Resolution, 5-Year Housing Plan)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda excluding Item 7, covering minutes, a TDA appointment, street acceptances, the Connecting Youth MOA (Item 6), bid reports, a swimming pool facilities assessment study with Sasaki Design, Leigh Farm Park design amendment #4, 411 Cleveland St roof renovations, Fire Station 9 design/testing amendments, a resolution supporting affordable housing around transit stations, street/sidewalk/waterline contracts, a yard waste facility contract amendment, an update to the five-year comprehensive housing strategy and dedicated funding plan, and UNRBA Falls Lake Stage 2 support.

agenda_items.title: Draft FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan for CDBG, HOME, and ESG Funds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers presented the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan allocating $1,795,508 in CDBG, $831,909 in HOME, and $147,357 in ESG funds, alongside local dedicated housing penny funds. Housing for New Hope staff, Rapid Rehousing clients (including the Glasper family), Urban Ministries, Durham Community Land Trustees, and Citizens Advisory Committee members testified in support of rapid rehousing and rental preservation. Councilmembers Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel questioned $192,000 in gap financing for Vermillion while praising a shift raising Habitat for Humanity second-mortgage assistance in Northeast Central Durham from $120,000 to $180,000; Council voted 7-0 to receive comments and then 7-0 to adopt the plan.

agenda_items.title: Amendments to FY 2011-2014 Annual Action Plans and CASA HOME Funds Award
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Wilma Conyers presented formal amendments reconciling $244,750 in HOME funds, $74,000 in CDBG funds, and $11,082 in ESG funds across FY 2011-2012, 2012-2013, and 2013-2014 Annual Action Plans to align with the general ledger and meet federal expenditure deadlines. With no public speakers, Council approved Item 26 unanimously 7-0 and immediately thereafter approved Consent Item 7 awarding HOME funds to Community Alternatives for Supportive Abodes (CASA) for permanent affordable housing 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to City-County Inspections Permit Fee Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City-County Inspections Director Jean Bradham presented targeted updates to the permit fee schedule, which had not been comprehensively adjusted since July 2011. The proposal left new single-family and new commercial permit fees unchanged while introducing a progressive plan-review resubmittal fee for uncorrected deficiencies, a first-reinspection fee for HVAC equipment replacements, and minor category fee increases and clarifications to recover inspection costs in line with peer cities. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment – UDI Farm (A14-00001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell recused himself from Items 28 and 29 as an employee of UDI CDC, turning the chair over to Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden. Pat Young presented UDI CDC's request to change the future land use map designation of 2.6 acres of a 5.9-acre site at 4601 Industry Lane from Office to Low Density Residential to permit urban agriculture and aquaponics (recommended 12-1 by the Planning Commission). Applicant attorney Patrick Byker explained that floodplain conditions prevented viable office development despite years of marketing.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change – UDI Farm (Z14-00001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden presiding, Pat Young presented UDI CDC's rezoning of 5.9 acres at 4601 Industry Lane from Office and Institutional (OI) to Residential Suburban 20 (RS-20) to allow an EDA-grant-funded commercial vegetable farm and aquaponics facility (recommended 12-1 by the Planning Commission). Attorney Patrick Byker, aquaponics specialist Kevin Hammock, and UDI President Ed Stewart answered council questions from Steve Schewel, Diane Catotti, and Don Moffitt regarding fish species (tilapia and perch), closed-loop water recycling and rainwater capture, 50-foot agricultural setbacks, odor absence, and projections to create 40 jobs over three years.

agenda_items.title: Street Closing – 127-Linear-Foot Right-of-Way Segment West of Chapel Hill Road (SC13-0006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented Case SC13-0006, a request by Beall's Design and Construction to close a 127-linear-foot right-of-way segment just west of Chapel Hill Road bordered by the applicant's property and Lakewood Elementary School, recombining 50% of the closed right-of-way to the applicant and 50% to Durham Public Schools. John Blakely of Edens Land Corp appeared on behalf of the applicant with no opposition from the public.

agenda_items.title: Police Department 2014 First Quarter Summary Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Jose Lopez reported a 36% increase in Part 1 violent crime (driven by 176 aggravated assault incidents involving 254 victims from multi-victim shootings into occupied dwellings and crowds), a 10% rise in property crime (burglaries and larcenies), a 13% rise in overall Part 1 index crime compared to Q1 2013's 14-year low, and slower priority-1 response times (6.1 minutes vs. 5.8-minute target), alongside drops in rape and auto theft and launch of the County Misdemeanor Diversion Program for 16- and 17-year-olds. Mayor Bell called the quarter a 'bad start' and requested individual offender counts behind the 304 juvenile offenses; Councilmembers Eddie Davis and Cora Cole-McFadden pressed Lopez on lack of diversity in the current police academy class and above-state academy requirements, while Steve Schewel, Eugene Brown, and Don Moffitt questioned violent crime tactics and diversion training.

votes.item_title: City Manager Priority Items (Hold Item 7 Until After Item 26; Add Supplemental Item 31)
votes.notes: Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden asked a follow-up question on Item 6 (Connecting Youth Durham County residency verification) without pulling the item.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented two priority agenda adjustments: holding Consent Item 7 (award of HOME funds to Community Alternatives for Supportive Abodes for permanent affordable housing) until after public hearing Item 26, and adding Supplemental Item 31 (Police Department 2014 Q1 Public Safety Report) to the agenda. Before voting, Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden clarified she did not wish to pull Consent Item 6 (Connecting Youth MOA) but asked whether the manager had followed up on how the program verifies that participating youth are Durham County residents; Bonfield replied he had inquired but did not yet have an answer. Council then voted 7-0 to approve the priority agenda adjustments.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Part 1): Close Public Hearing and Receive Citizen Comments on Draft FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan
votes.notes: Initial motion received public hearing comments; Council immediately took a second vote to formally adopt the plan.
votes.discussion_detail: After staff presented the draft FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan ($1.795M CDBG, $831.9K HOME, $147.4K ESG), seven speakers testified in support of rapid rehousing and rental preservation, including Housing for New Hope staff, previously homeless clients Tara and Demar Glasper, Durham Community Land Trustees director Selena Mack ($300,000 for 30 West End units), Citizens Advisory Committee member Shameka Rhinehart, Urban Ministries' Alexander Herring, and Frank Moore. Councilmembers Cole-McFadden, Moffitt, Catotti, Schewel, and Bell praised the shift increasing Habitat for Humanity second-mortgage funding in Northeast Central Durham from $120,000 to $180,000 (adding roughly four net units), while Catotti and Schewel raised concerns about $192,000 in gap financing for Vermillion and asked for deeper review when it returns individually. Council first voted 7-0 to receive the public hearing comments.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Part 2): Adopt FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan for CDBG, HOME, and ESG Funds
votes.notes: Required formal adoption vote after staff reminded Council the first vote only received comments; due to HUD by May 15.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after Council voted to receive public comments on Item 25, staff reminded Mayor Bell and Council that formal adoption of the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan was required for submission to HUD by the May 15 deadline. Staff confirmed that the adopted plan incorporated the May 1 supplemental memo adjusting the chart to increase homebuyer assistance from $120,000 to $180,000 to support at least nine Habitat for Humanity homebuyers in Northeast Central Durham, and that individual projects such as Vermillion would return separately for Council approval. Council moved, seconded, and unanimously adopted the Annual Action Plan 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Amendments to FY 2011-2012, 2012-2013, and 2013-2014 Annual Action Plans
votes.notes: Reconciles $244,750 in HOME, $74,000 in CDBG, and $11,082 in ESG funds to the general ledger.
votes.discussion_detail: Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers presented proposed amendments to the FY 2011-2012, 2012-2013, and 2013-2014 Annual Action Plans reconciling $244,750 in HOME funds, $74,000 in CDBG funds, and $11,082 in ESG funds to the city's general ledger in order to meet federal expenditure deadlines. Conyers certified newspaper, listserv, library, City Hall, and website public notice from April 4 through May 5. No council questions were raised and no members of the public spoke during the hearing. Council closed the public hearing and approved the amendments 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 7 (Deferred Consent): Award of HOME Funds to Community Alternatives for Supportive Abodes (CASA) for Permanent Affordable Housing
votes.notes: Taken up immediately after approval of Item 26 per City Manager's priority request.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the approval of prior-year HUD grant reconciliations in Item 26, Mayor Bell brought forward Consent Item 7, which awarded HOME funds to Community Alternatives for Supportive Abodes (CASA) for permanent affordable housing. The City Manager had asked Council to hold the item until after the Item 26 public hearing was completed. With no additional discussion needed, Council moved, seconded, and passed Item 7 unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Amendment to City-County Inspections Permit Fee Ordinance
votes.notes: Adds progressive plan-review resubmittal fee and first-reinspection fee for HVAC replacements; leaves new single-family and commercial permits unchanged.
votes.discussion_detail: City-County Inspections Director Jean Bradham presented targeted updates to the inspections permit fee ordinance, noting that new single-family residential and new commercial permit fees were unchanged. The amendments added a progressive fee for repeated plan reviews when applicants fail to correct noted deficiencies, added a reinspection fee on first reinspections of HVAC equipment replacements to encourage first-time compliance, and adjusted select trade permit fees to recover inspection costs in line with peer cities. Bradham confirmed outreach to homebuilders, general contractors, and mechanical/plumbing contractors. With no public speakers or council objections, Council closed the hearing and approved the ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Comprehensive Plan Amendment – UDI Farm (Case A14-00001)
votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell recused himself and abstained as an employee of applicant UDI CDC; Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden presided.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell excused himself from Items 28 and 29 due to his employment at UDI Community Development Corporation, and Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden assumed the chair. Planning staff member Pat Young presented Case A14-00001, changing the future land use designation of 2.6 acres of a 5.9-acre parcel at 4601 Industry Lane from Office to Low Density Residential to accommodate agricultural operations, noting a 12-1 Planning Commission approval recommendation. With no opposition, Council closed the public hearing and passed the plan amendment 6-0 with Bell abstaining.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Zoning Map Change – UDI Farm (Case Z14-00001)
votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell recused himself and abstained as an employee of UDI CDC; Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden presided.
votes.discussion_detail: With Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden presiding and Mayor Bell recused, Pat Young presented Case Z14-00001 rezoning approximately 5.9 acres at 4601 Industry Lane from Office and Institutional (OI) to Residential Suburban 20 (RS-20) to permit an aquaponics and commercial vegetable farming project funded by a federal Economic Development Administration grant (recommended 12-1 by the Planning Commission). Councilmembers Steve Schewel, Diane Catotti, and Don Moffitt questioned fish species, rainwater harvesting and tiered water rates, potential odor (none expected), and 50-foot agricultural setbacks, all of which staff and applicants addressed. votes.notes: Recombines closed right-of-way 50% to applicant Beall's Design and Construction and 50% to Durham Public Schools (Lakewood Elementary School).
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Case SC13-0006, a street-closing petition by Beall's Design and Construction for a 127-linear-foot right-of-way segment just west of Chapel Hill Road bordered by the applicant's property and Lakewood Elementary School on the north side. Upon closing, the right-of-way would be recombined equally, 50% to the applicant and 50% to Durham Public Schools. votes.item_title: Item 31 (Supplemental): Receive Police Department 2014 First Quarter Summary Report
votes.notes: Council requested follow-up data on unique juvenile offenders behind the 304 juvenile offenses and academy demographic tracking.
votes.discussion_detail: Police Chief Jose Lopez presented the Q1 2014 crime report, noting a 36% jump in Part 1 violent crime (176 aggravated assault incidents with 254 victims, heavily driven by shootings into occupied dwellings and crowds), a 10% rise in property crime, and a 6.1-minute priority-1 response time (missing the 5.8-minute target), alongside reductions in rapes and auto thefts and rollout of the Durham County Misdemeanor Diversion Program for 16- and 17-year-olds. Mayor Bell remarked that the city was 'not off to a good start' and asked for future reports to show how many unique youth accounted for the 304 juvenile offenses. Councilmembers Eddie Davis and Cora Cole-McFadden raised concerns about a lack of diversity in the current police academy class and asked about tracking candidates eliminated by credit, background, physical, or extra 300-hour academy standards, while Schewel, Brown, and Moffitt questioned violent crime tactics and diversion training. Council voted 7-0 to receive the report and comments.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting April 21, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on April 21, 2014, approving the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 7), extending an incentive deadline for The Gentian Group's Hotel Durham project, and voting 6-1—over Mayor Bell's dissent—to approve a $3.97 million, 15-year economic development incentive agreement with Austin Lawrence Partners East for the 26-story City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment. Bell argued the contract should guarantee a minimum annual property tax yield of $327,400, while the council majority and legal/finance staff warned that tying payments directly to tax yields risked violating state constitutional prohibitions on tax rebates and could jeopardize project financing. disagreements.issue: Austin Lawrence Partners (City Center / Jack Tar) Incentive Agreement – Minimum Guaranteed Property Tax Yield vs. Capital Investment Metric
disagreements.summary: Mayor Bill Bell dissented in a 6-1 vote on the $3.97 million, 15-year incentive agreement for the City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment, insisting the contract include an absolute minimum annual property tax yield ($327,400) rather than relying solely on capital investment thresholds, while the six council members and city finance/legal staff supported approving the agreement as drafted under existing policy.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the $3.97M incentive agreement immediately as drafted under existing economic development policy, relying on conservative tax assessor estimates ($60.9M assessed value) and avoiding constitutional tax-rebate risks.
side_a_arguments: Existing city policy bases incentives on qualified capital investment ($65M minimum) rather than actual tax revenue yields because directly linking incentives to tax revenues or requiring make-up payments risks violating the North Carolina Constitution's prohibition on tax rebates.

Finance staff already applied conservative buffers by basing projections on the tax assessor's $60.9M valuation (about 10% below the $65M minimum investment), capping the incentive at ~80.9% of projected property tax, and excluding ~$3.4M in projected hotel occupancy and sales taxes.
Delaying approval past April would disrupt the developer's imminent REIT financing term sheet and push back demolition and construction timelines.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hold the agreement until Thursday and amend Section 2.1 (or attach Exhibit D) to guarantee that the project generates at least $327,400 annually in general fund property tax revenue regardless of future property revaluations.
side_b_arguments: While the city's 15-year payout (~$265K/year) is fixed in dollars, future countywide property revaluations typically lower tax rates and could erode actual property tax inflows below the $327,400 projection.

Future councils paying out general fund dollars over 15 years should have contractual certainty of the minimum property tax revenue returning to the general fund rather than relying on non-binding memos or uncertain sales/hotel taxes.
disagreements.resolution: Council rejected Mayor Bell's request to hold the item until Thursday and approved the incentive agreement 6-1, with Bell voting No; City Attorney Fred Lamar agreed to examine revenue-guarantee mechanisms during the upcoming comprehensive Economic Development Policy overhaul.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presided over the April 10, 2014 Durham City Council Work Session, where Council unanimously accepted the City Manager's priority items—adding Bike-Ped Commission reporting, a citizen matter (John Tarantino), and a supplemental FY 2014 TIGER planning grant resolution. Ahead of the public hearing on Item 15 (proposed economic development incentives for Austin Lawrence Partners East LLC on West Parrish and West Main Streets), Council Member Steve Schewel pressed the developer and OEWD Director Kevin Dick for an earlier cleanup schedule for long-vacant burned-out Parrish Street buildings and stronger historic facade preservation beyond the McPherson Hospital outcome. Council also heard 2013 annual reports from the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission and Recreation Advisory Commission (asking the latter to identify the top five parks needing budget investment), and received an update from Public Works Manager Robert Joiner on the Failed and Struggling Developments program (now down to 83 projects across 23 subdivisions with roughly $8.5 million of infrastructure completed). Ernest Meals received all seven votes for a Workforce board appointment, and Council unanimously set the upcoming meeting agenda before adjourning at 2:59 p.m.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the work session to order at 1:00 p.m., with Bell, Diane Catotti, Eddie Davis, Don Moffitt, and Steve Schewel answering roll call (and Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden noting she would need to leave around 4:00 p.m.). The City Manager presented priority items—Item 10 (BPAC annual report), Item 18 (citizen matter John Tarantino), and Item 19 (FY 2014 TIGER planning grant resolution)—which Council unanimously accepted.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Review, Veterans Affordable Housing Discussion, and Item 15 (Austin Lawrence Partners Incentive)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk read consent and presentation items (including MCNC license, Baypoint/Green Gardens and Windemere Ridge CIP amendments, Campus Walk sidewalk grant, Bike-Ped and Recreation annual reports, and Failed/Struggling Developments) plus public hearings for the Durham Hotel (Tunisian Group LLC) and Austin Lawrence Partners East LLC (Item 15). Council praised a veterans and low-income housing project, and Council Member Steve Schewel flagged pre-hearing concerns on Item 15 regarding burned-out Parrish Street buildings, the July 2015 construction start, and preserving five historic facades better than McPherson Hospital.

agenda_items.title: Bicycle and Pedestrian and Recreation Advisory Commission 2013 Annual Reports
agenda_items.discussion_summary: BPAC representatives (supported by staff Dale McKeel) and the Recreation Advisory Commission (presentation credited to Susan Taylor) presented their 2013 annual reports on pedestrian/bicycle projects, park access, safety, and outreach. Council asked the Recreation Commission to return with its top five parks most in need of investment during budget deliberations.

agenda_items.title: Item 13: Failed and Struggling Developments Program Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Development Review Group Manager Robert Joiner reported passing one full year with no new developments entering the program, reducing active cases from 191 projects in 54 subdivisions at the 2009 peak to 83 projects in 23 subdivisions after completing ~40.5 miles of streets and ~40 stormwater facilities (~$8.5 million in infrastructure). He updated Council on Category 4 progress (Baypoint/Green Gardens repairs started, Windemere Ridge agreements advancing), Ravenstone/Stone Hill Estates litigation, and buyer outreach for Emory Woods.

agenda_items.title: Workforce Board Appointment, Agenda Setting, and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported that Ernest Meals received seven votes for the Workforce board appointment. Council unanimously set the upcoming meeting agenda (Consent Items 1–11 and 19; GBA public hearings Items 14–16), noted a 12:30 p.m. reducing-poverty meeting the next day, and adjourned at 2:59 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting April 7, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on April 7, 2014, presenting ceremonial recognitions including Little River Elementary fifth-grader Betty Closs (the region's first African American Duke Regional Spelling Bee champion) and a memorial resolution for civic and banking leader F.V. 'Pete' Allison Jr. Council approved a modified $2,400 window-easement agreement at 112 West Main Street, adopted the consent agenda, and unanimously approved the 105-unit Chapel Creek consolidated annexation and PDR 8.00 initial zoning near NC 54. Following extensive public comment from Healing with Care advocating broader access to homelessness funding, Council unanimously approved a rapid-rehousing contract amendment with Housing for New Hope while urging greater transparency in funding outreach, and amended and adopted FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines directing staff to study up to one cent per $100 valuation for parks and trails maintenance alongside municipal tax and fee comparisons.

Community Development's Larry Jarvis clarified the contract added FY 2014 funds ($200,000 dedicated housing penny and $67,000 ESG) as an extension to Housing for New Hope—the sole applicant in the publicized FY 2015 ESG/dedicated-fund round—whereas Healing with Care had applied through the separate Continuum of Care process, and Council members urged clearer outreach and simpler application communications before approving the contract 7-0.

Mayor Bill Bell opposed any new parks facilities or land banking, asked staff to raise the study ceiling to 1 cent for informational options while providing tax, fee, and solid-waste subsidy comparisons across North Carolina's largest cities plus Cary and Chapel Hill, and Cole-McFadden, Brown, and Moffitt raised questions about park security, cumulative fee burdens on low-income residents, and per-capita municipal revenues. Schewel acknowledged losing his push for new facilities (6-1) and moved an amendment directing staff to prepare a parks/trails maintenance and renovation plan at funding levels up to 1 cent (incorporating Cole-McFadden's park-policing question), which passed 7-0 before the full guidelines passed 7-0.

Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden raised concerns over protecting park assets through policing and cumulative rate impacts on low-income residents; Eugene Brown questioned shifting the $1.85 solid waste fee into a 0.4-cent property tax; and Don Moffitt requested per-capita local revenue comparisons. Acknowledging he lacked votes (6-1) for new parks facilities, Schewel moved to amend the guidelines so staff prepare a parks and trails maintenance and renovation plan at funding levels not to exceed 1 cent per $100 assessed value (including Cole-McFadden's security question), which passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 6 (Main Motion): Adopt FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines as Amended
votes.notes: Adopts full FY 2014-2015 budget guidelines following adoption of Schewel's parks maintenance amendment.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after passing Councilmember Steve Schewel's amendment directing staff to prepare parks and trails maintenance funding scenarios up to 1 cent per $100 assessed value (along with comparative municipal tax/fee data and park security information), Council proceeded to vote on the full amended FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines. With no further discussion, the motion was properly moved and seconded and passed unanimously 7-0.

disagreements.issue: FY 2014-2015 Budget Guidelines – Scope and Tax Level of Dedicated Parks Funding ('Penny for Parks')
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether dedicated property tax funding for parks should be used for new facilities and land expansion or restricted strictly to maintenance and renovation of existing assets, and weighed tax/fee burdens on lower-income residents before settling on an informational study capped at 1 cent solely for maintenance and renovation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Limit any dedicated parks funding strictly to maintaining and renovating existing parks and trails (no new facilities or land acquisition) and study up to 1 cent alongside peer-city tax/fee and park policing data.
side_a_arguments: Existing parks and recreation facilities face severe deferred maintenance deficiencies that must be addressed before building new facilities or buying land.
Raising taxes without clear maintenance priorities, police protection of park assets, and analysis of cumulative water/sewer/stormwater/solid-waste burdens could hurt low-income residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Seek new parks facilities in addition to maintenance and renovation (initially championed by Steve Schewel before conceding a 6-1 council majority against new facilities, shifting to a 0.5-cent maintenance/renovation study).
side_b_arguments: A majority of Council still supported exploring dedicated funding for parks and trails maintenance and renovation so Council could review concrete service-level options between 0 and 0.5 cents (or up to 1 cent) during budget workshops.
Underutilized small parks could also be evaluated for repurposing rather than purely selling or abandoning.
disagreements.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel conceded on record that his push for new parks facilities lacked support (6-1) and moved an amended guideline—approved 7-0—directing staff to present a specific plan for parks and trails maintenance and renovation at funding levels not to exceed 1 cent per $100 assessed value.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden opened the March 20, 2014 Durham City Council Work Session while Mayor Bill Bell was en route (with Bell presiding later in the session), and Council unanimously accepted priority items from the City Manager and City Attorney covering rapid-rehousing funding with Housing for New Hope, public art items, an Equal Business Opportunity Program extension, Council Procedures Subcommittee recommendations, and a 106 West Main Street air-rights easement. Following a middle transcript gap, Council debated Item 6 (FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines) and split 4-3 on a motion by Council Member Don Moffitt to add consideration of eliminating the solid waste fee and replacing it with up to 0.6 cents on the property tax rate (~$1.4 million): Don Moffitt was explicitly recorded in favor as the proposer/mover and Mayor Bill Bell was recorded among the three Nays (the remaining three Ayes and two Nays were not individually named in the transcript captions). After a subsequent motion for a half-cent parks funding target was withdrawn for lack of consensus, Council unanimously approved the budget guidelines including the solid waste consideration while directing staff to return before June with a list and cost estimate of parks deferred maintenance needs rather than setting a dedicated tax rate in the guidelines. Council then unanimously set the regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden called the work session to order while Mayor Bill Bell was on his way, with Cole-McFadden, Diane Catotti, Don Moffitt, and Steve Schewel noted during roll call. Council unanimously accepted the City Manager's priority items (suspending rules on Item 7 Housing for New Hope and Item 10 EBOP ordinance extension after presentation; presentations on Items 8–9) and the City Attorney's priority items (Council Procedures Subcommittee rules and Item 12 air-rights easement at 106 West Main Street).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review: Minutes, Social Media Audit, Housing for New Hope, and East End Connector
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk read consent items 1–16 and public hearing item 18, with members pulling Item 5 (Use of Social Media Performance Audit), Item 6 (Budget Development Guidelines), Item 7 (Housing for New Hope rapid-rehousing third amendment), and Item 16 (NCDOT East End Connector agreement). agenda_items.title: Item 6: FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines — Solid Waste Fee vs. Property Tax
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Don Moffitt moved to add to the FY 2014-2015 budget guidelines consideration of eliminating the solid waste fee and replacing it with up to 0.6 cents on the property tax rate (~$1.4 million), arguing it would replace a regressive fee with a less regressive tax. Opponents argued they did not support replacing the garbage fee with a property tax, and the City Attorney clarified the vote only placed the option in the guidelines for later budget consideration. The motion passed 4-3, with Don Moffitt confirmed in favor and Mayor Bill Bell named among the Nays.

agenda_items.title: Item 6: Budget Development Guidelines — Parks Maintenance and Final Guideline Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A motion to include up to a half-cent property tax consideration for Parks and Recreation maintenance drew objections from members who wanted to see the scope and dollar cost of deferred maintenance first and was withdrawn at 03:41:08. meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting March 17, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on March 17, 2014, celebrating Southern High School's 3AA state football championship, NCCU Chancellor Deborah Saunders White's upcoming installation, and NCCU's MEAC men's basketball championship alongside proclamations for Donate Life, CROP Hunger Walk, and Arbor Day. Council adopted the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 5) and then voted 6-1—with Eugene Brown dissenting—to uphold staff's denial of Phillips Research Park Apartments' $108,000 impact fee appeal after the City Attorney advised that City Code strictly required applying the 2009 fee schedule in effect when building permits were filed in 2010-2011 despite prolonged neighbor litigation. Council also held the FY 2014-2015 budget public hearing, approved the 54 Plaza annexation/CG(D) zoning and Bethpage Village committed-element revisions, adopted a memorial resolution for F.V. 'Pete' Allison Jr., authorized negotiations on $3.97 million in economic incentives for the City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment, and approved the pulled insurance plan.

agenda_items.title: Donate Life, CROP Hunger Walk, Arbor Day, Southern High Football, and NCCU Chancellor & Basketball Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell presented proclamations for Donate Life Month (Sharon Hirsch), the 40th annual Durham CROP Hunger Walk (Karen Johnson), and Arbor Day marking 31 years as a Tree City USA (Assistant General Services Director Chris Boyer). Council also honored the Southern School of Energy and Sustainability football team and Coach Adrian Jones for winning the 2013 NCHSAA 3AA state championship, recognized NCCU Chancellor Dr. Deborah Saunders White's installation by ceremonially naming Fayetteville Street 'NCCU Boulevard,' and celebrated Coach LeVelle Moton and the NCCU men's basketball team for winning the 2014 MEAC tournament.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (DPAC Appointments, FY 2013-14 Budget Amendments, SAMHSA Grant, Water Facility Chemical Systems)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the consent agenda excluding Item 5 (Annual Property and Casualty Insurance Plan 2014-2015), which was pulled by Victoria Peterson. Approved items included DPAC Oversight Committee appointments, FY 2013-2014 budget/grant/CIP ordinance amendments, a SAMHSA grant project ordinance and contract with Alliance Behavioral Healthcare, and a construction contract for North and South Durham Water Reclamation Facilities chemical systems.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing – Impact Fee Appeal, Phillips Research Park Apartments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson introduced an appeal under City Code Section 30-87 by Phillips Research Park Apartments seeking to apply pre-July 2009 impact fees ($108,000 lower) after neighbor Colonial's zoning appeal delayed site plan approval and caused Phillips to lose its 2008 loan before building permits were filed in 2010-2011. Attorney Robin Curren and developer Mr. Phillips argued for equitable tolling, while Planning Director Steve Medlin noted mandatory UDO stay rules and applicant-side delays, and City Attorney Patrick Baker advised Council had no legal basis in code to retroactively apply expired fees. Steve Schewel moved to uphold staff's assessment (seconded), Diane Catotti concurred, Eugene Brown urged referring back to the manager and criticized planning communication, Eddie Davis weighed splitting the fee difference, and Council voted 6-1 to uphold the staff determination with Brown voting No.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing – FY 2014-2015 Budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing to gather community input for the upcoming FY 2014-2015 budget. Seven speakers addressed Council: Victoria Peterson urged $5 million over five years for vocational-technical training at Holton School; DOST Chair LaDonna Summers urged budgeting Zone 2 impact-fee matching funds to prevent losing a nine-year-old $2 million federal rail-to-trail earmark; Vince Hammer, Donna Rudolph, John Martin, and Peter Katz of the InterNeighborhood Council advocated additional Planning Department staffing to complete the Wireless Facilities / Cell Tower Ordinance update and historic district grants; and Historic Preservation Commission Chair Heather Slane requested $2,000 for an annual historic-district newsletter.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation – 54 Plaza (Utility Extension, BDG13-14, Initial Zoning Z13-21)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Steve Medlin presented a consolidated utility extension agreement, voluntary contiguous annexation petition (BDG13-14), and initial Commercial General with a development plan zoning (Z13-21) for the 54 Plaza development, confirming adequate water/sewer capacity, immediate net-positive fiscal impact, and an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation. Brandon White of Kimley-Horn represented developer Durham Imperial Investors with no public opposition.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change – Bethpage Village Revisions (Z13-00030)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Steve Medlin presented committed-element revisions for Bethpage Village (PDR 4.733, IL(D), CG(D)) exempting Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA) units from voluntary DPS donations, modifying recreation amenities, and addressing an existing single grave site (recommended 11-0 by the Planning Commission). In response to concerns from Councilmember Don Moffitt and Diane Catotti, applicant representative Scott Lay proffered revised committed elements guaranteeing at least one active recreation area in any non-age-restricted portion and requiring HOA maintenance and a four-foot decorative fence with gate if the grave site is not relocated under state law.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Memorializing Ferdinand Vincent 'F.V. / Pete' Allison Jr.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted a supplemental resolution honoring the life, banking leadership, and civic contributions of Ferdinand Vincent 'F.V. / Pete' Allison Jr.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Economic Development Deal Points with Austin Lawrence Partners East, LLC (City Center & Jack Tar)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD's Kevin Dick presented preliminary deal points for an economic development incentive agreement of up to $3,970,095 over 15 years for Austin Lawrence Partners East's 26-story City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment, seeking authorization to negotiate a formal contract and schedule a G.S. 158-7.1 public hearing. Mayor Bill Bell objected to contract language stating 'no specific SDBE provisions are required by ordinance' and demanded firm minority contracting goals; Steve Schewel questioned how many of the 500 office jobs were relocated from Duke versus new, the gap between $71.5M taxable investment and $60.9M assessed value, Year 1 net fiscal return, combined city-county leverage ratio, livable wage, and minority hiring; and Cora Cole-McFadden pressed for summer youth employment participation (which Dick confirmed was embedded in the workforce plan).

agenda_items.title: Annual Property and Casualty Insurance Plan 2014-2015
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Item 5 had been pulled earlier by Victoria Peterson, who had already left the meeting by the time Council returned to the item. Council moved, seconded, and approved the insurance plan unanimously.

votes.notes: Item 5 (Annual Property and Casualty Insurance Plan 2014-2015) was pulled by Victoria Peterson.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bell read the consent agenda titles, including DPAC Oversight Committee appointments (Item 1), FY 2013-2014 budget, grant, and CIP ordinance amendments (Item 2), a SAMHSA grant project ordinance and contract with Alliance Behavioral Healthcare (Item 4), and a construction contract for North and South Durham Water Reclamation Facilities chemical systems (Item 6). Public speaker Victoria Peterson pulled Item 5 for separate discussion. With no council questions on the remaining items, Council approved the consent agenda 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 10: Impact Fee Appeal – Phillips Research Park Apartments (Uphold Staff / Committee Determination)
votes.notes: Upholds the Impact Fee Appeal Committee and staff determination applying the July 1, 2009 impact fee schedule ($108,000 higher than 2008 schedule) to building permits submitted in 2010-2011.
votes.discussion_detail: Budget Director Bertha Johnson presented the appeal under City Code Section 30-87 by Phillips Research Park Apartments, whose attorney Robin Curren and developer Mr. Phillips argued that a neighboring competitor's (Colonial's) Board of Adjustment and court appeals from 2008 to 2011 unfairly froze site plan approval, caused them to lose their 2008 loan, and subjected them to $108,000 in higher July 2009 impact fees when building permits were finally filed in 2010-2011. Planning Director Steve Medlin defended staff's compliance with mandatory UDO stay rules and noted long periods when the application awaited developer response, while City Attorney Patrick Baker and Inspections Director Jean Bradham advised that City Code strictly required calculating fees at completed building permit application with no legal basis to retroactively apply expired 2008 rates. Councilmember Steve Schewel moved to uphold staff's assessment (supported by Diane Catotti and Don Moffitt, who sympathized with the developer but said the city was not at fault), while Eugene Brown criticized Planning staff communication and requested deferral and Eddie Davis explored splitting the difference; Council passed Schewel's motion 6-1 with Brown voting No.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Close Public Hearing and Receive Comments on FY 2014-2015 Budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan
votes.notes: Receives resident public hearing comments on FY 2014-2015 budget priorities.
votes.discussion_detail: Seven speakers addressed Council during the FY 2014-2015 budget public hearing: Victoria Peterson urged $5 million over five years for vocational-technical training at Holton School; DOST Chair LaDonna Summers urged budgeting Zone 2 impact-fee matching funds to protect a $2 million federal rail-to-trail earmark nearing rescission; INC speakers Vince Hammer, Donna Rudolph, John Martin, and Peter Katz called for Planning Department staffing to complete the Wireless Facilities / Cell Tower Ordinance overhaul and historic district grants (prompting Councilmember Catotti and Mayor Bell to note the cell-tower rewrite was a major policy question rather than purely a staffing issue); and Historic Preservation Commission Chair Heather Slane sought $2,000 for an annual historic district newsletter. Council closed the public hearing and voted 7-0 to receive the comments.

votes.item_title: Item 12: Consolidated Annexation, Utility Extension, and Initial Zoning – 54 Plaza (BDG13-14 / Z13-21)
votes.notes: Approves utility extension agreement, voluntary contiguous annexation (BDG13-14), and initial CG(D) zoning (Z13-21) for 54 Plaza.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning Director Steve Medlin presented the consolidated utility extension agreement, voluntary contiguous annexation petition (BDG13-14), and initial Commercial General with a development plan zoning (Z13-21) for the 54 Plaza site, confirming adequate water and sewer capacity, immediate net-positive fiscal impact, and an 11-0 Planning Commission endorsement. Brandon White of Kimley-Horn appeared on behalf of developer Durham Imperial Investors and answered no opposing public comments as none were offered. Council closed the public hearing and approved the item 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Zoning Map Change – Bethpage Village Revisions (Case Z13-00030)
votes.notes: Amends committed elements for Bethpage Village (PDR 4.733, IL(D), CG(D)); exempts HOPA senior units from voluntary DPS donations.
votes.discussion_detail: Steve Medlin presented Z13-00030 modifying committed elements for Bethpage Village (originally approved by Durham County in 2007 and annexed in 2009) to exempt Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA) units from voluntary Durham Public Schools donations, alter recreation amenities, and address an existing single grave site (recommended 11-0 by the Planning Commission). Responding to concerns raised by Councilmember Don Moffitt and clarified by Diane Catotti, applicant representative Scott Lay proffered revised committed elements guaranteeing at least one active recreation amenity in non-age-restricted portions if the main recreation center is age-restricted, and preserving the grave site inside a four-foot decorative fence maintained by the HOA if next-of-kin prevent relocation under state law. Council closed the public hearing and passed the rezoning 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 14 (Supplemental): Resolution Memorializing Ferdinand Vincent 'F.V. / Pete' Allison Jr.
votes.notes: Resolution #987, subsequently presented ceremonially to Dr. E. Lavonia Ingram Allison at the April 7, 2014 meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bell introduced Supplemental Item 14, a resolution memorializing longtime Durham banking executive and community leader Ferdinand Vincent 'F.V. / Pete' Allison Jr. With no debate, the resolution was moved, seconded, and adopted unanimously 7-0.

votes.notes: Authorizes City Manager to negotiate an economic development agreement up to $3,970,095 over 15 years and hold a G.S. 158-7.1 public hearing on April 7 or April 21.
votes.discussion_detail: OEWD's Kevin Dick presented proposed deal points for an economic development incentive agreement with Austin Lawrence Partners East LLC for the 26-story City Center tower, historic facade restorations on Parrish and Main Streets, and the 74-room Jack Tar Motel and 260-space parking deck redevelopment, requesting authority to negotiate a formal contract up to $3,970,095 over 15 years and schedule a statutory public hearing. Mayor Bill Bell strongly criticized the draft's SDBE summary stating no specific SDBE provisions were required by ordinance and demanded specific minority participation goals before the agreement returned. Councilmember Steve Schewel probed whether the 500 office jobs included Duke relocations, why $71.5M in taxable improvements projected only $60.9M in assessed value, what Year 1 net revenues and combined city-county leverage ratios looked like, and urged ambitious livable wage and minority hiring targets, while Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden sought assurances on summer youth employment. Council approved authorizing negotiations and scheduling the public hearing 7-0.

votes.notes: Pulled earlier by Victoria Peterson, who departed before the item was called at the end of the meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: At the end of the meeting, Mayor Bell called Item 5, the Annual Property and Casualty Insurance Plan for 2014-2015, which had been pulled from the consent agenda by Victoria Peterson. Because Peterson had already left the chamber, no public comment was heard. Council moved, seconded, and approved Item 5 unanimously 7-0.

disagreements.issue: Phillips Research Park Apartments Impact Fee Appeal – Strict Code Enforcement vs. Equitable Tolling for Neighbor Litigation Delays
disagreements.summary: Council split 6-1 in upholding staff's denial of Phillips Research Park Apartments' appeal of a $108,000 impact fee increase incurred after a competitor's zoning appeals froze the project from 2008 until building permits were filed under the higher 2009 fee schedule, with Eugene Brown dissenting and Eddie Davis exploring a compromise split.
disagreements.side_a_position: Uphold the Impact Fee Appeal Committee and staff determination applying the July 1, 2009 impact fee schedule in effect when the building permit application was submitted.
side_a_arguments: City Code strictly mandates that impact fees be calculated at the time a completed building permit application is submitted (here 2010-2011), leaving Council and the Impact Fee Appeal Committee no legal authority to retroactively apply expired 2008 rates.
While the neighboring competitor's appeals caused hardship, Planning staff followed mandatory UDO stay provisions and the application also sat with the developer for extended periods.
Granting retroactive fee relief to one developer could expose the city to legal challenges and refund demands from other developers affected by fee or regulatory changes.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the appeal back to the City Manager rather than upholding the higher 2009 fee assessment, citing inadequate Planning Department communication and notification to the developer.
side_b_arguments: Planning staff failed to communicate effectively with the developer regarding the impact fee change and could have communicated more forcefully regarding the neighboring owner's interconnection obligations.

Because the developer relied on 2007 staff reliance letters, closed a $23 million loan in 2008, and was stalled by third-party litigation outside its control, Council should send the matter back to the Manager for further review rather than deny relief.
disagreements.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel's motion to uphold the staff and Impact Fee Appeal Committee determination passed 6-1, with Councilmember Eugene Brown voting No (while Councilmember Eddie Davis noted he would have favored splitting the increase in half if legally permissible but did not offer a substitute motion after Schewel's motion carried).

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting - Presentation on Police Headquarters/Annex and 911 Project Site Options
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell opened the March 13, 2014 Special City Council Meeting and turned over presiding duties to Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden upon his early departure. General Services Director Joel Reitzer, joined by Police, OEWD, Planning, Public Works, Transportation, Budget, and Finance staff, presented the administration's site evaluation for a new Police Headquarters/Annex and 911 facility, reviewing the Carter Goble and Associates 20–30 year space study, community outreach at Hayti Heritage Center, Golden Belt, and Downtown Durham Inc., and narrowing seven potential sites down to three primary options with reconciled cost estimates and construction timelines. Staff also analyzed trade-offs on a 19-acre Fayetteville Street corridor site—noting that dedicating 10 acres to law enforcement would only transfer jobs rather than generate new jobs and could make private mixed-use development of the remaining nine acres challenging. During public comment, speakers discussed Fayetteville Street manufacturing and job needs, while Preservation Durham Executive Director Wendy Harris echoed board member Rob Emerson in urging that the existing Milton Small-designed modernist Police Headquarters be sold as a historic property rather than demolished if vacated; no votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Public Comment Procedures
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the special meeting to order, had the clerk call roll (Diane Catotti, Eddie Davis, and Don Moffitt recorded answering; Bell, Cole-McFadden, Brown, and Schewel also called), outlined public comment rules, and announced Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden would conduct the remainder of the meeting after his early departure.

agenda_items.title: Staff Presentation: Police Headquarters/Annex and 911 Project Site Options
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services Director Joel Reitzer presented the multi-departmental site evaluation for a new Police Headquarters and 911 facility, referencing Carter Goble and Associates' 20–30 year space needs study, community meetings at Hayti Heritage Center and Golden Belt, and narrowing seven sites to three primary options with November/December cost reconciliations and construction schedules. Staff also evaluated a former housing authority / medium-density residential parcel and weighed opportunity costs along the Fayetteville Street targeted commercial corridor, noting 10 acres of law enforcement use could complicate private development on the remaining nine acres.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment on Police Headquarters Sites and Historic Preservation of Existing Building
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents spoke on job creation and environmentally friendly manufacturing needs along the Fayetteville Street corridor. Wendy Harris, Executive Director of Preservation Durham (1516 North Duke Street), echoed board member Rob Emerson and relayed concern from Triangle Modernist Houses and another modernist group, urging Council to sell the existing Milton Small-designed modernist police headquarters as a historic property rather than demolish it if the department relocates, before Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden closed the meeting.

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 6, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Rescheduled to Thursday afternoon at 4:30 p.m. after Monday's regular meeting was canceled and conducted briskly due to sleet outside, the Durham City Council approved the City Manager's priority deferrals of the FY 2014-2015 budget/CIP hearing and two land-use hearings to March 17, 2014. The Council unanimously adopted the 13-item Consent Agenda (including boards and commissions appointments, a performance audit, and infrastructure and sidewalk contracts) and approved General Business Item 19 without discussion. Police Chief Jose Lopez then delivered the Durham Police Department's 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report, highlighting national CALEA and forensic accreditations, a 6% drop in Part 1 violent crime (including a 23-year low in robberies), and a 6% increase in property crime driven by larcenies.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Weather Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the rescheduled March 6, 2014 meeting to order at 4:30 p.m., noting that Monday's meeting had been canceled and that council had already held work and closed sessions earlier in the day. All seven council members answered roll call. Mayor Bell announced that sleet was falling outside and urged council to move expeditiously for the safety of staff and attendees, adding that Southern High School's football team would be recognized on March 17.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items: Crime Report Presentation and Deferrals to March 17, 2014
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager's office requested to present supplemental Item 22 (Durham Police Department's 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report) during the meeting and to defer three public hearing items to March 17, 2014: Item 15 (FY 2014-2015 budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan), Item 16 (54 Plaza consolidated annexation), and Item 17 (Bethpage Village Revisions zoning map change Z1300030). Neither the City Attorney nor the City Clerk had priority items.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Appointments, Performance Audit, Infrastructure & Stormwater Contracts, Q2 Financial Report)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read the titles of Consent Agenda Items 1 through 13, covering minutes approval, appointments to the Appearance, Open Space and Trails, and Planning Commissions, street and infrastructure acceptances, a performance audit of inventory controls for tools and safety materials, Carver Street Extension right-of-way acquisition, DPR operations facility architectural amendment, Third Fork Creek stream restoration, ditching/pipe replacement, Garrett Road sidewalk construction, NCDOT Schedule C and D agreements, and the FY 2013-2014 Q2 financial report. No items were pulled by council or the public.

agenda_items.title: General Business Agenda Item 19
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following confirmation that public hearings Items 15 through 17 were deferred to March 17, 2014, Council took up General Business Agenda Item 19 without separate staff presentation or public comment. A motion to approve was immediately made, seconded, and carried unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Jose Lopez presented the 2013 annual crime summary, highlighting DPD's CALEA Gold Standard Accreditation, Forensics Services Division ISO accreditation, and outreach initiatives including the RAP burglary prevention program and mental health CIT outreach. Chief Lopez reported that Part 1 violent crime fell 6% in 2013 with robberies at a 23-year low and 30 criminal homicides (12 open), while property crime rose 6% due to larcenies (mostly thefts from vehicles and shoplifting), sworn staffing stood at 99% full at year-end, and average Priority 1 response time was 5.9 minutes against a 5.8-minute target. Council Member Don Moffitt noted the executive summary was missing from the packet and asked Chief Lopez to clarify the expanded FBI definition of rape (which accounted for the 40% statistical increase while prior-definition numbers held steady at 73) and the distinction between burglary and robbery.

agenda_items.title: Poverty Reduction Initiative Announcement and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell reminded council and the public about a follow-up meeting on his neighborhood-by-neighborhood poverty reduction initiative scheduled for March 19 from 7:30 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. at the Durham Rescue Mission, noting invitation letters had been sent to neighborhood associations. With no further business, the meeting adjourned at 4:49 p.m.

votes.item_title: City Manager's Priority Items (Present Item 22 Crime Report; Defer Items 15, 16, and 17 to March 17, 2014)
votes.notes: Deferred Item 15 (FY14-15 budget & FY15-20 CIP public hearing), Item 16 (54 Plaza annexation), and Item 17 (Bethpage Village Revisions Z1300030) to March 17, 2014; added Item 22 DPD Crime Report presentation.
votes.discussion_detail: Due to the rescheduling of the regular Monday council meeting to Thursday, March 6 at 4:30 p.m. and inclement sleet conditions, the City Manager's office proposed deferring three major public hearing items—the FY 2014-2015 budget and FY 2015-2020 CIP hearing (Item 15), the 54 Plaza consolidated annexation (Item 16), and the Bethpage Village Revisions rezoning Z1300030 (Item 17)—to the March 17, 2014 regular meeting. Staff requested to proceed only with presenting Supplemental Item 22, the Durham Police Department's 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report. No council members raised objections or requested discussion. Council unanimously approved the priority items 7-0.

votes.item_title: General Business Agenda Item 19
votes.notes: General Business Agenda Item 19 (not deferred; specific title not read aloud in transcript).
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following adoption of the Consent Agenda, Mayor Bill Bell called General Business Agenda Item 19 for action. No staff presentation, council questions, or public remarks were offered on the item, consistent with Mayor Bell's opening request to move swiftly because of worsening sleet outside. A motion to approve Item 19 was properly moved and seconded. The Council voted 7-0 to approve the item.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting (Due to cancellation of March 3, 2014 Meeting)
meetings.executive_summary: Held on Thursday, March 6, 2014 at 4:30 p.m. after inclement weather canceled the regular March 3 meeting (with Mayor Bill Bell noting sleeting conditions warranted moving expeditiously), the Durham City Council approved all action items unanimously by 7-0 votes. Council accepted the City Manager's priority items—hearing Item 22 (Durham Police Department 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report) immediately while deferring public hearings on Item 15 (FY 2015 budget and FY 2015–2020 CIP), Item 16 (54 Plaza consolidated annexation), and Item 17 (Bethpage Village revisions Z1300030) to March 17, 2014—and unanimously passed the 13-item Consent Agenda and General Business Agenda Item 19. Police Chief Jose Lopez presented the 2013 Crime Report, highlighting CALEA Gold Standard and ISO forensic accreditations, a 6% drop in Part I violent crime (1,625 incidents, with robberies at a 23-year low and 30 criminal homicides), a 6% rise in property crime driven by larcenies, an apparent 40% increase in rapes solely reflecting expanded FBI definitions (remaining flat at 73 under the prior definition), 99% sworn staffing, and a 5.9-minute average Priority 1 response time. Mayor Bell reminded Council of the March 19 Reducing Poverty meeting at the Durham Rescue Mission and adjourned at 4:49 p.m.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Priority Items (Deferral of Public Hearings 15–17)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the rescheduled March 3 meeting to order at 4:30 p.m. on March 6, noting sleet outside required prompt proceedings, with Eugene Brown leading the Pledge of Allegiance and all seven Council members present on roll call. Council voted 7-0 to approve the City Manager's priority items: presenting Item 22 today and deferring public hearings Items 15 (FY 2015 budget/CIP), 16 (54 Plaza annexation), and 17 (Bethpage Village Z1300030) to March 17, 2014.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–13) and General Business Agenda Item 19
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read consent Items 1–13—covering minutes, board appointments, street acceptances, an inventory/tools/safety materials audit, Carver Street right-of-way, DPR Operations Facility design amendment, Third Fork Creek stream restoration, ditching/pipe replacement, Garrett Road sidewalk SW-33, NCDOT Schedule C/D agreements, and the FY 2014 Q2 financial report—which passed 7-0. Council also approved General Business Agenda Item 19 by a 7-0 vote and confirmed Items 15–17 were deferred.

agenda_items.title: Item 22: Durham Police Department 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Jose Lopez reported CALEA Gold Standard and ISO forensic accreditation achievements alongside 2013 crime trends: Part I violent crime decreased 6% to 1,625 cases with robberies at a 23-year low and 30 criminal homicides (12 open), while property crime rose 6% due to vehicle-related larcenies and shoplifting. Lopez explained the 40% increase in reported rapes resulted from expanded FBI reporting definitions (holding flat at 73 under the old definition), noted 99% sworn staffing and 26 new BLET recruits, reported a 5.9-minute average Priority 1 response time, and answered Council questions on crime classification.

agenda_items.title: Announcements and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell reminded Council of the March 19 Reducing Poverty 'Neighborhood by Neighborhood' meeting from 7:30 to 10:00 a.m. at the Durham Rescue Mission and adjourned the meeting at 4:49 p.m.
